Clinical Reference

Status Epilepticus

On this page
A seizure lasting ≥5 minutes, or two or more seizures without return to baseline in between — a failure of the brain's own seizure-termination machinery. The brain becomes progressively harder to treat with every passing minute, so the clock, not the convulsion, is the emergency.
t1 = 5 min → treat now t2 = 30 min → neuronal injury Mortality ~9–21% (CSE); 23–61% (refractory) 1st line: a full-dose benzodiazepine 2nd line: LEV = fosphenytoin = valproate (ESETT)
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — why a seizure refuses to stop

Every seizure you have ever seen that stopped on its own stopped because the brain's inhibitory machinery won. Synaptic GABA-A receptors — chloride channels that hyperpolarize neurons — clamp down on the runaway excitation and the seizure self-terminates, usually in under two minutes. Status epilepticus is what happens when that machinery fails.

And here is the part that makes status epilepticus different from every other seizure: it actively destroys its own treatment. Within minutes of a seizure becoming self-sustaining, two things happen in parallel at the synapse:

  • Synaptic GABA-A receptors are endocytosed — physically pulled out of the membrane and internalized into the cell. The brakes are not just being overwhelmed; they are being removed. Benzodiazepines work by binding GABA-A receptors, so as those receptors disappear from the synapse, benzodiazepines lose potency — on the order of ~20-fold over the first tens of minutes. This is time-dependent pharmacoresistance, and it is the single most important concept in this disease.
  • NMDA and AMPA (glutamate) receptors are trafficked toward the synapse — the accelerator is being installed. Excitation climbs while inhibition collapses.

The consequences follow directly. Excess Ca²⁺ pours through NMDA receptors, activating calpain and caspase cascades → excitotoxic neuronal death, hitting the hippocampal CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons hardest. Meanwhile the body's compensation fails: in the first ~30 minutes a catecholamine surge keeps cerebral blood flow matched to the enormous metabolic demand (Phase 1 — hypertension, tachycardia, hyperglycemia, lactic acidosis). After ~30 minutes cerebral autoregulation breaks down, blood flow becomes passively pressure-dependent while demand stays maximal (Phase 2) — supply and demand decouple, and neurons die. Systemically you now get hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, and pigment-induced acute kidney injury.

A seizure is a fire. Normally the sprinkler system (GABA-A) puts it out in seconds. In status epilepticus, the fire is ripping the sprinkler heads out of the ceiling as it burns — and simultaneously opening more gas lines (NMDA/AMPA). Your benzodiazepine is water aimed at sprinkler heads that are no longer there. That is why the same drug that would have worked at minute 3 fails at minute 40 — and why the correct response to "the benzo didn't work" is almost never "give another benzo," but "move down the ladder, fast."
The failure-of-termination cascade. The two purple boxes — GABA-A receptors leaving the synapse, NMDA/AMPA receptors arriving — are the engine of pharmacoresistance and the reason every minute of delay matters.

The receptor-trafficking clock — the single graph that explains the whole disease

Read this as the pharmacology of the emergency: benzodiazepine efficacy is a decaying function of time, while the NMDA-receptor population — ketamine's target — is a rising one. The treatment ladder is built to follow those two curves.

Schematic (not to scale) of the receptor-trafficking basis of time-dependent pharmacoresistance in status epilepticus. Direction and relative timing follow the mechanism described in the NCS 2012 guideline and the ILAE 2015 t1/t2 rationale; the curves are illustrative, not measured data.
The GABA-A receptor — the benzodiazepine target that status epilepticus removes from the synapse.

Every drug, mapped to the step it interrupts

This table is the through-line of the entire guide. When you pick a drug, you are picking a step in the cascade above to attack.
Drug / classMolecular targetWhat it actually doesWhere it sits in the cascade
Benzodiazepines
lorazepam, midazolam, diazepam		GABA-A receptor (BZD site)Positive allosteric modulator — increases the FREQUENCY of Cl⁻ channel opening. Needs GABA present, and needs the receptor to still be in the membrane.Restores inhibition — but only while the receptors are still there. Hence: give it EARLY and give it FULL-DOSE.
Phenytoin / fosphenytoinVoltage-gated Na⁺ channelUse-dependent block of fast inactivation — preferentially silences neurons that are firing rapidly, i.e. the seizing ones.Cuts the high-frequency firing that sustains the seizure. Does not touch GABA at all — which is why it still works when benzos are failing.
Levetiracetam / brivaracetamSV2A (synaptic vesicle protein 2A)Modulates presynaptic vesicle release — dampens the output of the excitatory terminal. Not a channel blocker.Turns down glutamate release upstream. Minimal drug interactions, not hepatically metabolized.
ValproateMulti-targetNa⁺ channels + T-type Ca²⁺ channels + increases GABA availability (↑ synthesis / ↓ degradation).Hits both sides of the balance — why it is especially good in generalized and myoclonic epilepsy.
LacosamideVoltage-gated Na⁺ channelEnhances SLOW inactivation — a mechanistically distinct action from phenytoin's fast-inactivation block, so it can be additive with it.Second Na⁺-channel lever. Watch the PR interval.
Phenobarbital / pentobarbitalGABA-A receptor (barbiturate site)Increases the DURATION of Cl⁻ channel opening — and at high concentrations can open the channel directly, without GABA.This is the key: barbiturates do not depend on the same receptor pool or on GABA being present the way benzos do — so they can still work after benzos have failed.
PropofolGABA-A (+ Na⁺ channel)Potent GABA-A agonist with rapid on/off kinetics — titratable to burst-suppression within minutes.Anesthetic-depth seizure suppression. Beware propofol infusion syndrome.
KetamineNMDA receptor antagonistBlocks the glutamate receptor that status epilepticus has been actively adding to the synapse. Also sympathomimetic → does not drop the blood pressure.The mechanistically correct drug for late/refractory SE: as GABA drugs get weaker with time, ketamine's target gets more abundant.
Pyridoxine (vitamin B6)GAD cofactorCofactor for glutamic acid decarboxylase, the enzyme that makes GABA from glutamate. Isoniazid poisons it.The antidote in INH overdose and pyridoxine-dependent seizures — SE that will not stop until you give it.
MagnesiumNMDA channel porePhysically plugs the NMDA channel; also membrane-stabilizing.The specific therapy in eclampsia — superior to phenytoin in that setting.

Definitions, timing, and stages — get these exactly right

The ILAE 2015 conceptual definition (Trinka et al., Epilepsia) is built on two time points: t1, when the seizure is unlikely to stop on its own and you must start treating; and t2, beyond which long-term consequences (neuronal death, network injury) become likely.

Seizure typet1 — start treatmentt2 — injury beginsWhat that means at the bedside
Generalized tonic-clonic (convulsive) SE5 min30 minYou have 5 minutes, not 30. Treat at 5.
Focal SE with impaired awareness10 min>60 minSlightly more time, but the same trajectory.
Absence SE10–15 minUnknownILAE lists t2 as not established. Benign relative to CSE — do not intubate and anesthetize an absence SE.

The NCS 2012 guideline operationalizes this simply: SE = 5 minutes or more of continuous clinical and/or electrographic seizure activity, OR recurrent seizure activity without recovery (return to baseline) between seizures.

StageDefinitionWhat you doMortality
Impending / early SESeizure ≥5 minFull-dose benzodiazepine—
Established SE (ESE)Seizure persists after an adequate benzodiazepineSecond-line ASM (levetiracetam / fosphenytoin / valproate)CSE overall: 9–21% at discharge
Refractory SE (RSE)SE that does not respond to the standard regimen — i.e. fails a benzodiazepine + one second-line ASM (NCS 2012)Intubate + continuous IV anesthetic + cEEG23–61% at discharge
Super-refractory SE (SRSE)SE that continues or recurs ≥24 h after starting IV anesthesia, including recurrence on weaning the anestheticKetamine, add-on ASMs, immunotherapy, ketogenic diet, inhaled anesthetics~30–50% long-term
NORSENew-Onset Refractory SE: RSE in a patient without active epilepsy and without a clear acute structural, toxic, or metabolic cause. ~50% remain cryptogenic; the rest are largely autoimmune/paraneoplastic.Aggressive hunt for autoimmune encephalitis; early immunotherapyHigh
FIRESFebrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome — a subset of NORSE preceded by a febrile illness between 2 weeks and 24 hours before onset of RSEAs NORSE + consider anakinra / tocilizumab, ketogenic dietHigh
NCSENon-convulsive SE: seizure activity on EEG without the clinical findings of convulsive SE. Two phenotypes: the "wandering confused" ambulatory patient (better prognosis) and the critically-ill comatose patient with subtle or no motor signs (worse).You cannot diagnose it without an EEG.18–52% at discharge
The most dangerous form of status epilepticus is the one you can't see. Up to a third of patients whose convulsions stop are still seizing electrically. If a patient does not begin waking up within ~20–30 minutes of the convulsions stopping, assume non-convulsive status epilepticus and get an EEG — do not write it off as "post-ictal."

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Signs & symptoms — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Split every finding into three buckets: (1) the seizure itself, (2) the catecholamine surge of Phase 1, and (3) the systemic decompensation of Phase 2. Frequencies below are approximate, pooled from convulsive-SE cohorts and the NCS 2012 / AES 2016 evidence base; they are teaching anchors, not precise epidemiology.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Impaired consciousness (does not return to baseline between seizures)~100%Definitional. Widespread cortical + thalamic recruitment prevents normal arousal networks from re-forming. Failure to return to baseline is the single most useful bedside sign.
Generalized tonic-clonic convulsions~70–80%
of SE presentations		Bilateral synchronous cortical discharge recruiting corticospinal tracts. Tonic phase = sustained depolarization; clonic phase = the discharge being intermittently interrupted by (failing) inhibition. As SE goes on, convulsions become subtler — the motor signs fade before the electrical seizure does.
Tachycardia + hypertension (early)~80%Phase 1 catecholamine surge. Massive sympathetic outflow. Cerebral blood flow rises to match a 2–3× jump in metabolic demand. Later, this reverses into hypotension — a falling BP in SE is a late, ominous sign.
Lactic acidosis~70–80%Anaerobic metabolism in violently contracting muscle + catecholamine-driven glycolysis. Lactate can exceed 10 mmol/L. It self-corrects within ~1 hour of seizure control — do not chase it with bicarbonate and do not reflexively call it sepsis.
Hyperglycemia (early) → hypoglycemia (late)~50–60%Catecholamines + cortisol drive glycogenolysis early. With prolonged SE, glycogen is exhausted and hyperinsulinemia persists → late hypoglycemia, which then perpetuates the seizure. This is why the fingerstick is not optional.
Hyperthermia~40–60%Heat generated by sustained muscle contraction + central thermoregulatory disruption. Not the same as fever from infection — but you cannot tell them apart at the bedside, so it does not excuse you from looking for meningitis.
Elevated CK / rhabdomyolysis~40–50%Sustained contraction → sarcolemmal injury → myoglobin release → pigment nephropathy and hyperkalemia. Peaks 24–72 h after the event, so a normal initial CK does not exclude it.
Leukocytosis (peripheral, and CSF pleocytosis)~40–60%Catecholamine-driven demargination. A seizure alone can produce a mild CSF pleocytosis — but you can never attribute pleocytosis to the seizure without excluding CNS infection first.
Todd's paralysis (post-ictal focal deficit)~15–30%Regional neuronal exhaustion + active inhibition in the cortex that was seizing. Lasts hours to days. Mimics stroke — and a stroke can also cause the seizure, so image the brain.
Aspiration / hypoxemia~20–30%Loss of airway protection during the convulsion + impaired ventilation during the tonic phase + copious secretions.
Subtle motor signs only (nystagmus, eye deviation, face/finger twitching) — "subtle SE"~15–25%
of ICU SE		Electromechanical dissociation: the brain is still seizing but the motor output has decoupled after prolonged SE. The most missed presentation. Requires EEG.
Neurogenic pulmonary edema~5–10%Catecholamine storm → intense pulmonary venoconstriction + capillary stress failure. Presents as sudden hypoxemia with a white chest X-ray after prolonged SE.
Cardiac arrhythmia / Takotsubo~5–10%Catecholamine toxicity to myocardium. Troponin can rise without coronary disease.
Tongue laceration (lateral)~5–15%Tonic masseter contraction. Lateral tongue biting is fairly specific for a generalized tonic-clonic seizure; tip-of-tongue biting is not, and is common in PNES.

■ >70%   ■ 40–70%   ■ 15–40%   ■ <15%

Convulsions stopping is not the same as the seizure stopping. As SE persists, motor manifestations progressively fade while the electrical seizure continues (electromechanical dissociation). "He stopped shaking" is reassuring only if he also starts waking up.

Is this really an epileptic seizure? — psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES)

PNES is common, is not volitional, and is dangerous to get wrong in both directions: intubating and barbiturate-coma-ing a PNES patient is a catastrophic iatrogenic injury; dismissing true SE as PNES is fatal. No single sign is definitive — the definitive test is an EEG during the event.

FeatureFavors epileptic seizureFavors PNES
Movement patternSynchronous, rhythmic, decreasing frequency with time; stereotypedAsynchronous, out-of-phase, waxing/waning; side-to-side head shaking; pelvic thrusting; opisthotonic arching
DurationUsually <2–3 min per seizureOften prolonged (>5–10 min), fluctuating
EyesOpen during the eventForcefully closed, resists passive opening
Post-ictalConfusion, somnolence, gradual recovery; lateral tongue bite; incontinenceRapid return to baseline; recall of the event; emotional distress
PhysiologyLactate rises, prolactin may rise, post-ictal acidosis, hypoxemiaNormal lactate, no acidosis; preserved O₂ sat
Response to ASMResponds (early)Does not respond — escalating anesthesia in a "refractory" patient who is really PNES is the classic disaster
A normal serum lactate drawn shortly after a "generalized tonic-clonic seizure" should make you seriously reconsider the diagnosis — real convulsive activity is metabolically expensive and almost always raises it. It is supportive evidence, not proof.
🧠

The EEG — what you are actually looking at

EEG is not an optional adjunct in status epilepticus. It is the only instrument that tells you whether your treatment worked, and it is the sole way to diagnose the non-convulsive forms. Learn to read the montage and the two patterns that matter.

The International 10-20 system. Odd numbers = left hemisphere, even = right; Fp/F/C/T/P/O = frontopolar, frontal, central, temporal, parietal, occipital. Reading the montage is what lets you say where the discharge arises — which is what points you at the etiology.
Brylie Christopher Oxley, CC0 — Wikimedia Commons: International 10-20 system for EEG-MCN.png
Generalized spike-and-wave discharges across all channels with abrupt onset and offset — the electrographic signature of a generalized non-convulsive (absence) seizure. Continuous discharges like this in a patient who is not waking up = non-convulsive status epilepticus.
Bromfield EB, Cavazos JE, Sirven JI (eds.), CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons: EEG Absence seizure.png
Burst-suppression (top trace): high-voltage bursts punctuating long stretches of near-flat suppression (<1 µV, shaded), versus a continuous, non-suppressed background below. This is the titration endpoint for continuous anesthetic infusions in refractory SE — and it is a target you literally cannot dose to without continuous EEG.
Kleinhern, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons: Fneur-12-750667-g001.jpg (cropped to the EEG panel)

Diagnosing non-convulsive SE — the Salzburg Consensus Criteria

The Salzburg criteria (Leitinger et al.) are the accepted framework for calling NCSE on EEG; in a three-centre validation published in Lancet Neurology (2016) they had a sensitivity of ~98% and specificity of ~90%. The operational logic, in brief:

  • Epileptiform discharges >2.5 Hz → NCSE.
  • Epileptiform discharges ≤2.5 Hz, OR rhythmic delta/theta activity (>0.5 Hz), → NCSE only if one of the following is ALSO present: (a) clinical and EEG improvement after an IV ASM; (b) subtle clinical ictal phenomena time-locked to the discharge; or (c) typical spatiotemporal evolution of the pattern.
  • Patients with a known epileptic encephalopathy are judged against their own baseline (an increase in discharge frequency/prominence with observable clinical change).
The IV-ASM trial ("benzodiazepine trial") is a legitimate diagnostic manoeuvre for the ambiguous EEG: give a test dose of a benzodiazepine while recording, and look for both resolution of the EEG pattern and clinical improvement. EEG improvement without clinical improvement is not a positive test — sedation alone can flatten a rhythmic pattern.

Terminology note: rhythmic and periodic patterns that are neither clearly ictal nor clearly interictal (LPDs, GPDs, LRDA) sit on the ictal–interictal continuum (IIC) — a concept formalized in the ACNS 2021 Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology. Whether these patterns cause independent brain injury and warrant aggressive anesthesia is genuinely unsettled; the NCS guideline explicitly calls it controversial. Escalating to burst-suppression for an IIC pattern alone is a decision to make with neurology, not reflexively.

🖼️

Imaging — what to order, when, and what it shows

Imaging in status epilepticus answers a single question: what is causing this, and does it need something other than an anticonvulsant? The CT is for the things that will kill the patient in the next hour. The MRI is for the things that will kill them in the next week — and it is far more sensitive for essentially every cause of new-onset SE.

StudyWhen to order itWhat you are looking forWhat it changes
Non-contrast head CT Essentially every patient ("appropriate for most cases" — NCS 2012), as soon as they are stable enough to travel. Do not delay treatment for it. Intracranial hemorrhage, large infarct, mass with midline shift, hydrocephalus, herniation, skull fracture. Fast, and rules out the things that change the next 60 minutes. Hemorrhage → neurosurgery, reverse anticoagulation. Mass/shift → dexamethasone, neurosurgery. Also clears the way for a safe LP.
MRI brain, with & without contrast
(epilepsy protocol: thin coronal T2/FLAIR through the hippocampi)		 New-onset SE with a non-diagnostic CT; focal semiology; suspected encephalitis or autoimmune disease; any refractory SE without a cause. Within 24–48 h. Mesial temporal sclerosis, focal cortical dysplasia, encephalitis, tumour, PRES, small infarct, cortical laminar necrosis (post-anoxic). The highest-yield test for finding the actual cause of new SE. A routine (non-epilepsy-protocol) MRI will miss both hippocampal sclerosis and cortical dysplasia — ask for the protocol by name.
Peri-ictal MRI changes (a trap, not a diagnosis) Seen incidentally on an MRI done during or shortly after prolonged SE. Cortical/hippocampal DWI restriction, T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, and leptomeningeal enhancement caused by the seizure itself — from cytotoxic edema and hyperperfusion. It typically crosses vascular territories and involves the ipsilateral pulvinar/thalamus. Do not call it a stroke and do not call it encephalitis. These changes are usually reversible and often resolve on repeat imaging. Recognizing them prevents an unnecessary thrombolysis decision — but they are a diagnosis of exclusion, so treat the infection you cannot exclude.
CT angiography / venography Suspected stroke, dissection, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (seizure + headache + a hemorrhagic infarct that does not respect an arterial territory, especially peripartum or in a thrombophilia). Large-vessel occlusion; venous sinus filling defect. CVST is a cause of SE that is treated with anticoagulation — an answer you will never reach by escalating anticonvulsants.
CT chest / abdomen / pelvis + pelvic or testicular ultrasound NORSE, or any suspicion of autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis. Ovarian teratoma (classic in anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis); small-cell lung cancer; thymoma; testicular germ-cell tumour. Removing the teratoma treats the disease. This is one of the very few places in super-refractory SE where a surgeon can cure the patient.
Chest X-ray Routinely after convulsive SE. Aspiration (common) and neurogenic pulmonary edema. Antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia; ventilatory support.
Left hippocampal (mesial temporal) sclerosis — volume loss and signal change in the left hippocampus compared with the normal right. It is both a cause of drug-refractory focal epilepsy (and therefore of SE) and a consequence of prolonged seizures — the CA1/CA3 excitotoxic injury from the pathophysiology section, made visible. It is also the lesion that resective surgery cures.
Uhomachinky, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons: Left Hippocampal Sclerosis on MRI.jpg
HSV encephalitis — asymmetric T2 hyperintensity of the medial temporal lobe and insula. A classic cause of new-onset SE, and the one you must not miss: start empiric acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h on suspicion, before the PCR returns. Untreated HSV encephalitis has a mortality above 70%; treated early, it is survivable.
Dr Laughlin Dawes, CC BY 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons: Hsv encephalitis.jpg
Peri-ictal MRI changes are the great mimic. Prolonged seizure activity itself produces cortical DWI restriction and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity — which looks like a stroke, or like encephalitis. The tells: it crosses vascular territories, often involves the ipsilateral pulvinar, and resolves on repeat imaging. Knowing this stops you thrombolysing a seizure. Not knowing it means you will.

The lab panel — why each number moves

LabDirectionMechanism — and what fools you
Lactate↑↑↑ (can exceed 10)Anaerobic metabolism in convulsing muscle + catecholamine-driven glycolysis. Clears within ~1 h of seizure control. Falsely reassuring: a normal lactate after an apparent GTC seizure should make you reconsider the diagnosis (think PNES). Falsely alarming: it looks like sepsis, and it isn't. Genuinely alarming: a lactate that does not clear — that is an ongoing seizure, sepsis, ischemic bowel, or PRIS.
Glucose↑ early, ↓ lateCatecholamines and cortisol drive glycogenolysis early; with prolonged SE, glycogen exhausts while hyperinsulinemia persists → late hypoglycemia, which then perpetuates the seizure. Hypoglycemia is also a cause of SE. Check it first, always.
CK↑↑Sarcolemmal injury from sustained contraction. Peaks at 24–72 h — a normal CK on arrival does NOT exclude rhabdomyolysis. Recheck it. CK >5000 → aggressive IV fluids.
Potassium↑Released from injured myocytes (rhabdomyolysis) and shifted out by acidosis. Careful: this makes succinylcholine risky for intubation after prolonged convulsive SE.
Creatinine↑Pigment (myoglobin) nephropathy + pre-renal from volume loss and hyperthermia. Tea-coloured urine, dipstick positive for blood, but no RBCs on microscopy = myoglobinuria.
WBC↑ (and CSF pleocytosis)Catecholamine-driven demargination — not infection. But a seizure can also cause a mild CSF pleocytosis, and you may NEVER attribute pleocytosis to a seizure until you have excluded CNS infection. Treat first, attribute later.
pH / bicarbonate↓ (lactic acidosis)Consequence of the lactate. Self-corrects within ~1 h of seizure control. Do not give bicarbonate; do not hyperventilate.
ASM level↓ (subtherapeutic)The single most common precipitant in a known epileptic. The trap: a "low" total phenytoin in a hypoalbuminemic patient may be a toxic free level — order the free phenytoin.
Sodium↓ (as a cause)Hyponatremia lowers the seizure threshold and is a classic reversible cause. No ASM will fix a sodium of 118 — hypertonic saline will. Also drug-induced: carbamazepine and (more so) oxcarbazepine cause SIADH.
Ammonia↑ (if on valproate)Valproate causes hyperammonemic encephalopathy with completely normal LFTs and a therapeutic drug level. If a valproate patient is not waking up, send an ammonia before you blame the seizure.
Troponin↑Catecholamine-mediated myocardial injury / Takotsubo — can rise without any coronary disease. Do not reflexively cath a post-SE troponin rise; get an echo and look at the ECG.
Prolactin↑ (unreliably)Post-ictal hypothalamic-pituitary discharge. Must be drawn 10–20 min post-event with a baseline; useless beyond ~6 h; does not reliably rise in focal or non-convulsive seizures; and a normal value NEVER excludes a seizure. Low yield — do not build a decision on it.

The clock — master treatment algorithm

⏱️

Time-based algorithm (AES 2016 / NCS 2012)

This one figure is the disease. Definitive control of SE should be established within 60 minutes of onset (NCS 2012). Every box below is a deadline, not a suggestion — the phases exist because the pharmacology changes underneath you.

Master algorithm for convulsive status epilepticus. Doses from AES 2016 (Glauser), NCS 2012 (Brophy, Tables 7–8), and ESETT (Kapur, NEJM 2019). Full dose ladders, alternatives, and comorbidity adjustments are in the Wards and ICU panels.
The #1 error in status epilepticus is benzodiazepine UNDERDOSING — a reflexive "lorazepam 1 mg or 2 mg IV" in an 80 kg adult who needs 0.1 mg/kg = 4 mg (the max per dose), repeatable once. Under-dosing the first drug converts a treatable seizure into a refractory one, because you have spent the window in which benzodiazepines still work. NCS 2012 explicitly links inadequate therapy — insufficient dose, wrong route, delay between treatments — to mortality as high as 45%, versus 8% with adequate therapy.
🩺 Clinic — preventing status epilepticus before it happens
Assess

Who is about to have status epilepticus

🔍

The clinic patient on the road to SE

You almost never see status epilepticus in clinic. What you see in clinic is the patient who is going to have it next month — and your job is to identify and defuse them. Roughly half of all SE occurs in people with known epilepsy, and in that group the most common precipitant is sub-therapeutic anti-seizure medication (ASM) levels — non-adherence, a missed refill, a new interacting drug, or an inappropriate taper. That is a clinic problem, and it is preventable.

Warning sign in clinicWhy it predicts SEWhat to do about it today
Missed doses / ran out of medicationThe commonest precipitant of SE in known epilepsy. ASM levels fall below threshold and the seizure network is disinhibited.Check a level. Fix the supply chain (90-day fills, mail order, pill box, alarms). Ask non-judgmentally — "most people miss doses; how many did you miss this week?"
Seizure clusters / acute repetitive seizures (≥2–3 in 24 h, distinct from their usual pattern)Clusters are the direct precursor of SE — the termination machinery is already faltering.Prescribe a rescue medication and write a seizure action plan. This is the highest-yield thing you will do in the visit.
Rising seizure frequency / breakthrough on a stable regimenA new precipitant has entered the picture (drug interaction, sleep deprivation, alcohol, infection, pregnancy, a progressive lesion).Level + medication reconciliation + hunt the new variable. Consider re-imaging if the semiology has changed.
A new interacting drug (rifampin, an antiretroviral, a new oral contraceptive, an enzyme inducer/inhibitor)Silently drops the ASM level. Oestrogen-containing contraceptives cut lamotrigine levels by ~50%; enzyme inducers slash levels of many ASMs.Recheck the level 1–2 weeks after any interacting drug is started or stopped.
Alcohol use disorderWithdrawal seizures cluster and progress to SE. Also drives non-adherence, hypoglycemia, thiamine deficiency, and head trauma.Screen (USPSTF Grade B). Treat the AUD. Note: phenytoin does NOT prevent alcohol-withdrawal seizures — benzodiazepines do.
Abruptly stopped an ASM, benzodiazepine, or barbiturateWithdrawal seizures. Never stop an ASM abruptly.Always taper. Restart and taper properly.
PregnancyVolume of distribution and clearance rise → ASM levels fall, sometimes steeply (especially lamotrigine and levetiracetam).Monitor levels each trimester; dose up pre-emptively; taper back down postpartum. Co-manage with neurology/MFM.
Progressive symptoms (new focal deficit, headache, personality change, weight loss)A structural or autoimmune cause is evolving — tumour, autoimmune encephalitis, HSV.Urgent MRI ± referral. Do not simply up-titrate the ASM.
The question "do you have a rescue medication at home, and does the person who lives with you know how to give it?" is the most valuable question in an epilepsy follow-up visit — and the one most often skipped. A benzodiazepine given at home at minute 5 is worth more than anything you can do at minute 50 in an ICU.

What to order & when

🧪

Outpatient labs & imaging

ASM drug levelAny breakthrough seizure, any cluster, any suspected non-adherence, after any interacting drug change, each trimester in pregnancy. Draw a trough (just before the next dose). In a known epileptic this is the single highest-yield test you can send.Core
CMP + Mg + ionized Ca + PhosAny new or breakthrough seizure. Hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypoglycemia, and uremia all lower the seizure threshold and are all correctable causes — no ASM will fix a sodium of 118.Core
CBCBaseline and monitoring: valproate → thrombocytopenia; carbamazepine → leukopenia, aplastic anemia.Core
LFTs + ammoniaBaseline before valproate — and whenever a valproate patient becomes encephalopathic. Valproate causes hyperammonemic encephalopathy with normal LFTs and a therapeutic drug level. Send an ammonia, not just an AST.If on VPA
β-hCGAny person of childbearing potential, before starting or changing an ASM. Valproate and topiramate are teratogens.Core
25-OH vitamin D ± DEXALong-term enzyme-inducing ASMs (phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine) accelerate vitamin D catabolism → osteomalacia and fracture. Check vitamin D; DEXA per risk (see USPSTF panel).Chronic
MRI brain — epilepsy protocolAny first unprovoked seizure; any change in semiology; any new focal deficit; drug-resistant epilepsy. Ask explicitly for thin coronal T2/FLAIR through the hippocampi — a routine brain MRI will miss mesial temporal sclerosis and focal cortical dysplasia.Structural
Routine / ambulatory EEGClassify the epilepsy as focal vs generalized — this decides which drug you may safely use. Also for spells of uncertain nature and suspected absence. A normal routine EEG never excludes epilepsy.Classify
Video-EEG monitoring (epilepsy unit)Spells not responding to ASMs (rule out PNES); pre-surgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy (failed ≥2 appropriately chosen, adequately dosed ASMs).Referral

Interpreting the ASM level — the part people get wrong

DrugTherapeutic rangeWhat moves it — and how it fools you
Phenytoin (total)10–20 µg/mLThe classic trap. Phenytoin is ~90% albumin-bound and only the free fraction is active. In hypoalbuminemia, uremia, pregnancy, or critical illness the total level reads low-or-normal while the free level is toxic. Kinetics are zero-order in the therapeutic range — a small dose increase can produce a large, non-linear jump in level.
Phenytoin (free)1–2 µg/mLJust order the free level. Correction equations (Sheiner–Tozer) exist, but the published coefficients disagree with each other and the equations have been shown to be biased and imprecise in critically ill, head-injured, and renal patients. A measured free level beats any correction. (If you must estimate: MDCalc corrected-phenytoin calculator.)
Valproate50–100 µg/mLAlso highly protein-bound. Can cause encephalopathy through hyperammonemia at a perfectly therapeutic level — the number does not tell you the patient is toxic. Also: thrombocytopenia, pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity, weight gain, tremor, alopecia.
Carbamazepine4–12 µg/mLAuto-induces its own metabolism over 2–4 weeks — the level you achieve at first will fall on its own and needs a dose increase. Also causes hyponatremia (SIADH), leukopenia, and is a strong inducer that wrecks other drug levels.
Phenobarbital15–40 µg/mLVery long half-life (~4 days) — steady state takes weeks, so do not chase levels early. Strong enzyme inducer.
Levetiracetam, lacosamide, lamotrigineNo well-established population rangeLevels here establish this individual's effective baseline and confirm adherence — they are not targets to titrate to. A "therapeutic" number means "the number this patient was well at."
A phenytoin level of 8 µg/mL in a patient with an albumin of 2.0 is not necessarily subtherapeutic — it may be toxic. Order the free phenytoin, and do not reflexively load more drug into a hypoalbuminemic patient who is ataxic and nystagmoid.
Treat

Prevention: the rescue plan & the chronic ladder

🚨

Step 1 — the home rescue medication (this is what actually prevents SE)

Home rescue benzodiazepines exploit the one window in which benzodiazepines remain maximally potent — before the GABA-A receptors have been internalized. A caregiver giving intranasal midazolam at minute 5 is doing pharmacologically what a paramedic does, an hour earlier and far more effectively. That is why the outpatient visit matters for a disease that presents in the ED.
AgentStartRepeat ruleCeilingWhy it worksIf unsuitable / alternative
Midazolam nasal spray
(Nayzilam)		 5 mg — one spray into one nostril One further 5 mg spray into the OPPOSITE nostril after 10 min if no response 2 doses per episode. Do not treat >1 episode every 3 days, or >5 episodes/month GABA-A positive allosteric modulator. Nasal mucosa gives rapid absorption with no IV needed. Approved ≥12 y. Do not give the second dose if there is breathing difficulty or excessive sedation. Alternative: diazepam nasal or rectal.
Diazepam nasal spray
(Valtoco)		 0.2 mg/kg if ≥12 y  (0.3 mg/kg if 6–11 y; 0.5 mg/kg if 2–5 y).
For ≥12 y by weight: 14–27 kg → 5 mg; 28–50 kg → 10 mg; 51–75 kg → 15 mg; ≥76 kg → 20 mg		 A second dose may be given after at least 4 hours (use a new blister pack) 2 doses per episode. Do not treat >1 episode every 5 days, or >5 episodes/month GABA-A PAM. Approved ≥2 y. The 15 mg and 20 mg doses are given as one spray in each nostril. Nasal congestion can impair absorption — keep rectal gel as backup.
Diazepam rectal gel
(Diastat)		 0.2–0.5 mg/kg PR, age-banded (NCS 2012: 2–5 y → 0.5 mg/kg; 6–11 y → 0.3 mg/kg; ≥12 y → 0.2 mg/kg) May repeat once per the prescribing plan Typically 20 mg per dose The long-standing generic option. Works when there is no IV and no nasal option; absorption is reliable. Dignity and practicality issues in adults and in public — nasal sprays are usually preferred where affordable.
Buccal midazolam 0.5 mg/kg buccal (NCS 2012) Per plan ~10 mg typical Absorbed across the buccal mucosa; widely used outside the US. Not an FDA-approved product in the US; availability varies.
Clobazam
(daily adjunct, not an abortive)		 5–10 mg/day ↑ 5–10 mg/day at roughly weekly intervals as tolerated 20–40 mg/day divided BID A 1,5-benzodiazepine — reduces cluster frequency as a maintenance drug. Sedation, tolerance. Not a substitute for a rescue medication.

The seizure action plan — write it down, give them a copy

  1. Protect. Roll them on their side, cushion the head, nothing in the mouth, clear hazards. Do not restrain.
  2. Time it. Look at a clock. This is the instruction caregivers most often fail to follow, and it is the one that determines everything downstream.
  3. At 5 minutes of continuous convulsion — or at a second seizure without recovery in between — give the rescue medication.
  4. Call 911 if: the seizure continues ≥5 min after the rescue dose; a second dose is needed; another seizure follows without full recovery; breathing is laboured or the skin is dusky; it happened in water; there is injury; it is a first-ever seizure; the person is pregnant or diabetic; or they do not return to their normal self.
💊

Step 2 — the chronic ASM ladder (the other half of prevention)

The first fork is the only one that really matters: is this FOCAL or GENERALIZED epilepsy? Getting it wrong is not merely ineffective — phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin, pregabalin and (with caution) lacosamide can WORSEN absence and myoclonic seizures, and have precipitated absence status epilepticus. If you are not certain, get an EEG before committing to a sodium-channel blocker.
1
First-line monotherapy — chosen by syndrome
SANAD II (Lancet 2021) is the trial that settles this
▾

SANAD II — two open-label non-inferiority RCTs (~1,510 patients), and the answer is not the one most residents expect:

  • Focal epilepsy (n=990): levetiracetam failed non-inferiority against lamotrigine (HR 1.18, 97.5% CI 0.95–1.47, against a margin of 1.329); zonisamide met it (HR 1.03). Lamotrigine also had far fewer adverse reactions (33% vs 44% LEV / 45% ZNS), fewer psychiatric effects (13% vs 30% / 23%), and dominated on cost-effectiveness. → Lamotrigine remains first-line for focal epilepsy.
  • Generalized / unclassified epilepsy (n=520): levetiracetam failed non-inferiority against valproate (HR 1.19, 95% CI 0.96–1.47, margin 1.314). → Valproate remains first-line for generalized epilepsy — but only where pregnancy is not a possibility (≈10% major congenital malformation rate plus dose-dependent neurodevelopmental harm).
DrugStartTitration incrementsTarget / maxWhy it worksMonitor / if intolerant
Lamotrigine
1st-line FOCAL		 25 mg daily × 2 weeks → 50 mg daily × 2 weeks → then ↑ 50 mg every 1–2 weeks 200–400 mg/day divided BID Na⁺-channel blockade + reduced glutamate release. Best-tolerated first-line agent; safe in pregnancy. SJS/TEN. The slow titration is the safety feature — never rush it, and never restart at the old dose after a gap. Any rash → stop and call.
Lamotrigine with valproate 25 mg EVERY OTHER DAY × 2 weeks → 25 mg daily × 2 weeks → ↑ 25–50 mg every 1–2 weeks ~100–200 mg/day — roughly half the usual target Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation and roughly doubles its level. This combination sharply increases SJS risk — halve every step. Conversely, enzyme inducers (CBZ, PHT, phenobarbital, rifampin) roughly double the dose required.
Valproate
1st-line GENERALIZED		 10–15 mg/kg/day divided ↑ 5–10 mg/kg/day each week Level 50–100 µg/mL; max ≈60 mg/kg/day The broadest spectrum drug: Na⁺ channels + T-type Ca²⁺ channels + increased GABA. The best agent for myoclonic and absence seizures. Contraindicated in pregnancy/childbearing potential without ironclad contraception, and in POLG/mitochondrial disease (fatal hepatotoxicity). Also: hyperammonemia, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, weight gain, tremor, alopecia, PCOS.
Levetiracetam
the pragmatic workhorse		 500 mg BID ↑ 1000 mg/day every 2 weeks Max 3000 mg/day — no added benefit above this per the FDA label SV2A modulation. No hepatic metabolism, essentially no interactions, IV:PO 1:1, no levels needed — which is why it dominates hospital practice despite SANAD II. Behavioural/psychiatric effects (~30% in SANAD II) — irritability, aggression, depression. Ask at every visit. Renal dose adjustment required. Alternative: brivaracetam — same SV2A target, better psychiatric tolerability.
Zonisamide 100 mg daily ↑ 100 mg every 2 weeks 100–400 mg/day Na⁺ + T-type Ca²⁺ channels, plus carbonic-anhydrase activity. Met non-inferiority vs lamotrigine in SANAD II. Contains a sulfonamide moiety — avoid in sulfa allergy. Renal stones, weight loss, oligohidrosis, metabolic acidosis, cognitive slowing.
What if you don't know their home dose? Don't guess and don't withhold. Send a drug level, then restart at a conservative, standard starting dose of the same agent (e.g. levetiracetam 500 mg BID; lamotrigine must be restarted from the beginning of the titration schedule if more than ~5 half-lives have lapsed, or you risk SJS). Call the dispensing pharmacy — it is usually faster than any other route and gives you the actual dispensed dose and last fill date, which also tells you about adherence.
2
If the first drug fails — switch, then add
Second monotherapy, then rational polytherapy
▾

Failed for intolerance → switch to a different first-line agent (cross-titrate: bring the new one up before taking the old one down). Failed for lack of efficacy at an adequate dose → try a second monotherapy, then move to combination therapy, pairing agents with different mechanisms (a Na⁺-channel drug + an SV2A drug, rather than two Na⁺-channel drugs).

DrugStartTitration incrementsTarget / maxWhy it worksMonitor / if intolerant
Lacosamide50 mg BID↑ 100 mg/day each week200–400 mg/day divided BID (up to 600 mg/day)Enhances SLOW Na⁺-channel inactivation — mechanistically distinct from phenytoin/carbamazepine, so it can be combined with them.PR prolongation — get an ECG; avoid in 2nd/3rd-degree AV block. Dizziness, diplopia. IV form available at 1:1 with PO.
Brivaracetam50 mg BIDAdjust within the range by response and tolerability25–100 mg BID (50–200 mg/day)High-affinity SV2A ligand — the same target as levetiracetam with ~20× the affinity.The go-to when levetiracetam works but its behavioural side effects are intolerable. IV form available.
Oxcarbazepine300 mg BID↑ 600 mg/day each week1200–2400 mg/day divided BIDNa⁺-channel blocker; the keto-analogue of carbamazepine, with less enzyme induction and no auto-induction.Hyponatremia — more than carbamazepine. Check a sodium. Worsens myoclonic/absence seizures. Test HLA-B*15:02 before use in patients of Han Chinese or Southeast Asian ancestry (SJS/TEN risk).
Carbamazepine200 mg BID↑ 200 mg/day each week800–1200 mg/day; level 4–12 µg/mLThe prototypical use-dependent Na⁺-channel blocker; highly effective in focal epilepsy.Auto-induces its own metabolism — the level falls at 2–4 weeks and needs re-dosing. Strong CYP3A4 inducer (wrecks warfarin, DOACs, OCPs, antiretrovirals). Hyponatremia, leukopenia, aplastic anemia. HLA-B*15:02 → SJS/TEN. Worsens myoclonus/absence.

Always dose at night. Can be given by NG tube in the ICU.

Notably high seizure-freedom rates in drug-resistant focal epilepsy.The glacial titration is mandatory — it exists to prevent DRESS, which occurred with faster schedules. Do not accelerate it.
