Gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, ataxia, nystagmus, osteomalacia, cerebellar atrophy, DRESS. Strong enzyme inducer. Rarely a modern first-line outpatient choice.
3
Drug-resistant epilepsy — stop adding drugs, refer
Failed ≥2 appropriately chosen, adequately dosed ASMs
▾

ILAE definition: failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen, adequately dosed ASM schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom. After two failures, the probability that a third drug delivers seizure freedom falls into the single digits. Adding a fourth agent is not a plan — it is a delay.

  • Refer to a comprehensive epilepsy centre for video-EEG. Two questions get answered there: are these even epileptic seizures? (a meaningful fraction of "refractory epilepsy" turns out to be PNES) and is there a resectable focus?
  • Resective surgery — e.g. anterior temporal lobectomy for mesial temporal sclerosis. In well-selected patients this is dramatically more effective than any further drug trial.
  • Neuromodulation when resection isn't possible: vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), responsive neurostimulation (RNS), or DBS of the anterior thalamic nucleus.
  • Ketogenic / modified Atkins diet — effective in selected patients, and also a rescue option in super-refractory SE.
  • Re-examine the diagnosis: autoimmune epilepsy (LGI1, CASPR2, GAD65, NMDA-R antibodies), a missed structural lesion, or a genetic/metabolic syndrome.
Every year a patient with a resectable mesial temporal focus spends on a fourth ASM is another year of seizures, another year of SE risk, and another year of hippocampal injury. Two failed drugs is a referral, not a third drug.
Monitor

Titration, follow-up & life with epilepsy

📈

What to recheck, and when

WhenWhat you checkWhy
2–4 weeks after starting or changing an ASMSymptoms, side effects, adherence, rash. CBC/LFTs if on valproate or carbamazepine. Level if the drug has one.This is when idiosyncratic reactions appear — rash progressing to SJS, cytopenias, hepatitis. Lamotrigine rash risk peaks at 2–8 weeks.
At steady state (≈5 half-lives)Trough level, to establish this patient's effective baseline number.The number you will compare against forever after. Especially valuable for phenytoin, valproate, carbamazepine.
Every 3–6 months once stable (6–12 months if seizure-free ≥1 y)Seizure diary, side effects, adherence, mood screen, contraception/pregnancy plans, driving status.The mood screen is not optional — depression and suicidality are markedly increased in epilepsy and are worsened by levetiracetam, topiramate, and perampanel.
After ANY breakthrough seizureLevel + metabolic panel + medication reconciliation + precipitant hunt (sleep, alcohol, illness, new drug, missed doses).A breakthrough seizure is a warning shot for status epilepticus. Find the reason — don't just raise the dose.
Each trimester in pregnancy, and postpartumASM levels — especially lamotrigine and levetiracetam.Clearance rises steeply → levels fall → breakthrough seizures. Dose up during pregnancy, then taper back down postpartum or you will make her toxic.
Annually on enzyme-inducing ASMs25-OH vitamin D, calcium; DEXA per risk.Phenytoin, phenobarbital, and carbamazepine induce vitamin D catabolism → osteomalacia, osteoporosis, fracture.

🚗 Driving

Rules are jurisdiction-specific; most US states require a seizure-free interval of 3–12 months before driving resumes. A minority of states mandate physician reporting. Document the counselling at every visit. This is both a legal obligation and a safety intervention — and patients consistently report that no one ever had the conversation with them.

🤰 Pregnancy & contraception

  • Avoid valproate (≈10% major malformations plus dose-dependent IQ reduction) and topiramate (orofacial clefts) in anyone who could become pregnant.
  • Preferred: lamotrigine, levetiracetam.
  • Folic acid — USPSTF Grade A: 0.4–0.8 mg daily for anyone who could become pregnant.
  • Enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, oxcarbazepine, topiramate ≥200 mg) reduce oral-contraceptive efficacy → use an IUD or a depot method.
  • Conversely, oestrogen-containing contraceptives cut lamotrigine levels by ~50% → breakthrough seizures when the pill starts, and toxicity in the pill-free week.

💀 SUDEP — you have to say the word

Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy is the leading cause of epilepsy-related death in people with uncontrolled generalized tonic-clonic seizures. The strongest modifiable risk factor is the frequency of GTC seizures — which means adherence and seizure control are the intervention. Nocturnal seizures and sleeping alone raise the risk. Guidance supports discussing SUDEP explicitly: patients want to know, and the disclosure improves adherence. Do not let it be the thing nobody mentioned.

Interact

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

⚠️

How each comorbidity changes the disease AND the drug you pick

ComorbidityHow it changes the diseaseHow it changes managementAvoid / use with caution
Cirrhosis / liver disease Hepatic encephalopathy lowers the seizure threshold and mimics NCSE. Impaired metabolism and low albumin distort free-drug levels. Prefer levetiracetam (renally cleared, no hepatic metabolism) or lacosamide. Order free phenytoin, never total alone. Valproate — hepatotoxicity and hyperammonemia. Caution with phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital.
CKD / ESRD Uremia lowers the seizure threshold; dialysis disequilibrium can provoke seizures; altered protein binding raises free phenytoin. Levetiracetam must be renally dose-adjusted (FDA label): CrCl >80 → 500–1500 mg q12h; 50–80 → 500–1000 q12h; 30–50 → 250–750 q12h; <30 → 250–500 q12h; ESRD on dialysis → 500–1000 mg q24h plus a 250–500 mg supplemental dose after each session. Levetiracetam, phenobarbital, and gabapentin are substantially dialyzed — redose after HD. Un-adjusted levetiracetam → somnolence and obtundation that gets mistaken for NCSE. Total phenytoin levels are actively misleading here.
Hypoalbuminemia (any cause) Doesn't change the seizure — changes your reading of it. Order a FREE phenytoin level. Trusting a total phenytoin level. Correction equations disagree with one another and are imprecise in exactly the patients who need them.
Heart failure / arrhythmia / heart block Cardiac arrest and hypoperfusion cause hypoxic-ischemic SE — often myoclonic, and prognostically grim. For established SE, pick levetiracetam or valproate over fosphenytoin. ESETT showed all three are equally effective — so choose on the side-effect profile, and this is exactly the patient in whom that matters. Fosphenytoin/phenytoin — hypotension and arrhythmia (rate-related; the propylene glycol diluent in IV phenytoin is a major culprit). Lacosamide — PR prolongation; avoid in 2nd/3rd-degree AV block.
Pregnancy SE risk is not increased by pregnancy itself, but falling ASM levels cause breakthrough seizures. Always think eclampsia. Rapid maternal seizure control is what protects the fetus — do not withhold treatment. NCS 2012 recommends lorazepam and fosphenytoin, and states levetiracetam should be considered. For eclampsia: magnesium sulfate is superior to phenytoin — 4–6 g IV over 15–20 min, then 1–2 g/h — and delivering the fetus is the definitive therapy. Check vitamin B6 (may be low in pregnancy). Valproate (~10% major malformations), topiramate (clefts), phenobarbital. Phenytoin is teratogenic but acceptable acutely when it is the right drug.
Alcohol use disorder Withdrawal seizures (typically 6–48 h after the last drink) cluster and progress to SE. Brings thiamine deficiency, hypoglycemia, hypomagnesemia, head trauma, and liver disease with it. Benzodiazepines are both the treatment and the prophylaxis — symptom-triggered (CIWA) dosing. Give thiamine 100 mg IV BEFORE glucose (glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's). Replete magnesium. Phenytoin does NOT prevent or treat alcohol-withdrawal seizures. This is a well-established negative finding and a classic ward error. Do not reach for it.
HIV / immunocompromised Broadens the differential enormously — toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus, PML, CNS lymphoma, TB, HIV encephalopathy. Image and LP with a very low threshold. Prefer levetiracetam or lacosamide (minimal interactions). Enzyme-inducing ASMs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital) lower protease-inhibitor and NNRTI levels → virological failure and resistance.
Mitochondrial disease / POLG mutation Presents as refractory SE, classically in a young patient with a NORSE-like picture and hepatic involvement (Alpers syndrome). Keep a high index of suspicion in unexplained refractory SE in a young person. VALPROATE IS CONTRAINDICATED — it precipitates fulminant, often fatal, hepatic failure in POLG mutation. This is the single most important "never" on this page.
Generalized epilepsy (absence / myoclonic / JME) An entirely different pharmacology from focal epilepsy. Use valproate (or levetiracetam; lamotrigine can worsen myoclonus in some patients). Phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin, pregabalin, and (with caution) lacosamide can WORSEN absence and myoclonic seizures — and have precipitated absence status. Getting the syndrome wrong actively harms the patient.
Acute porphyria Attacks present with seizures plus abdominal pain and neuropsychiatric features. Safe options: levetiracetam, gabapentin. Treat the porphyria (hemin, glucose). Phenytoin, barbiturates, carbamazepine, valproate — all porphyrinogenic; all can precipitate an attack.
Elderly / frailty SE incidence is highest at the extremes of age, and presentation in the elderly is far more often non-convulsive — mistaken for delirium, dementia, or stroke. Lower starting doses, slower titration. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are best tolerated. Have a low threshold for EEG in unexplained encephalopathy. Enzyme inducers (polypharmacy interactions, bone loss, falls). Sedating agents (falls).
Anticoagulated (warfarin / DOAC) A seizure with a fall becomes an intracranial hemorrhage. Use a non-inducing ASM: levetiracetam, lacosamide, brivaracetam. Enzyme inducers lower DOAC levels → thrombotic failure, and unpredictably swing the warfarin INR.
Depression / psychiatric illness Highly prevalent in epilepsy; independently raises SUDEP and suicide risk; also raises the chance that PNES coexists with the epilepsy. Screen at every visit (USPSTF Grade B). SSRIs are generally safe in epilepsy — the old fear that they "lower the seizure threshold" is overblown at therapeutic doses. Levetiracetam, perampanel, topiramate (behavioural/psychiatric effects). Bupropion and clozapine genuinely do lower the seizure threshold in a dose-dependent way — avoid, or use with great care.
The "never" list — drugs to avoid, by situation
  • Valproate + POLG / mitochondrial disease → fatal hepatic failure. Absolute contraindication.
  • Valproate or topiramate in pregnancy or childbearing potential without reliable contraception → teratogenesis.
  • Phenytoin / carbamazepine / oxcarbazepine / gabapentin in generalized (absence, myoclonic) epilepsy → worsens the seizures.
  • Phenytoin for alcohol-withdrawal seizures → it does not work. Use benzodiazepines.
  • Lacosamide in 2nd/3rd-degree AV block → PR prolongation and heart block.
  • Fosphenytoin/phenytoin in the hypotensive or bradyarrhythmic patient → choose levetiracetam or valproate; ESETT says they are equivalent, so there is no efficacy price to pay.
  • Enzyme-inducing ASMs with antiretrovirals, DOACs, warfarin, oral contraceptives, chemotherapy, or transplant immunosuppressants → failure of the other drug.
  • Carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine in patients of Han Chinese or Southeast Asian ancestry without HLA-B*15:02 testing → SJS/TEN.
  • Any barbiturate, phenytoin, carbamazepine, or valproate in acute porphyria → precipitates an attack.
  • Abruptly stopping any ASM or benzodiazepine → withdrawal seizures and SE.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B recommendations that actually apply to the epilepsy patient

These are not generic health-maintenance filler. Each one maps onto a real driver of seizure risk, ASM safety, or mortality in this specific population. Grades are from the USPSTF A & B recommendation list, current as of January 2025.

GradeRecommendationPopulationWhy it matters in epilepsy
AFolic acid supplementation, 0.4–0.8 mg dailyAll persons planning or able to become pregnantASMs are teratogens and several are folate antagonists. The highest-yield preventive act in a young person with epilepsy.
ATobacco cessation — ask, advise, and provide behavioural intervention plus FDA-approved pharmacotherapyAll non-pregnant adults who use tobaccoDrives the cerebrovascular disease that causes adult-onset seizures and SE. Caveat: bupropion lowers the seizure threshold — prefer varenicline or NRT in this population.
AHypertension screening with office BP, confirmed outside the clinic before starting treatmentAdults ≥18 yThe dominant modifiable risk factor for stroke — and stroke is a leading cause of adult-onset epilepsy and of SE.
AHIV screeningAdolescents & adults 15–65 y (plus others at increased risk)HIV massively broadens the seizure differential (toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus, PML, lymphoma) and creates critical ASM–antiretroviral interactions.
BUnhealthy alcohol use screening + brief behavioural counsellingAdults ≥18 y, including pregnant personsAlcohol withdrawal is a leading precipitant of SE, and drives non-adherence, trauma, thiamine deficiency, and liver disease.
BDepression screeningAll adults, including pregnant/postpartum and older adultsStrikingly prevalent in epilepsy; worsened by levetiracetam, topiramate, perampanel; drives suicide and non-adherence → SE.
BAnxiety disorder screeningAdults ≤64 y, including pregnant/postpartumSame axis as depression; also a major driver of PNES, which coexists with epilepsy more often than people expect.
BFalls prevention — exercise interventionsCommunity-dwelling adults ≥65 y at increased riskSeizures cause falls; sedating ASMs cause falls; enzyme-inducing ASMs thin the bone that then breaks. A triple hit in the elderly epileptic.
BOsteoporosis screening with bone measurement testingWomen ≥65 y; postmenopausal women <65 y at increased riskEnzyme-inducing ASMs accelerate vitamin D catabolism → osteomalacia and fracture. Long-term ASM use is an increased-risk factor.
BHepatitis C screeningAdults 18–79 yIdentifies the liver disease that changes ASM selection (valproate, phenytoin) and alters drug metabolism.
BIntimate partner violence screeningWomen of reproductive ageHead trauma causes epilepsy; IPV is also a barrier to adherence and to safe storage of rescue medication.

Not USPSTF, but do it anyway: keep immunizations current (infection is a seizure precipitant); counsel on sleep (deprivation is among the most reliable seizure triggers); and counsel on safety — showers rather than baths, never swim alone, care with heights, ladders, and open flames.

Escalate

When to send them to the ED

🚑

Red flags — do not manage these in clinic

  • Any seizure lasting ≥5 minutes, or ≥2 seizures without return to baseline in between — this is status epilepticus. Call 911; give the rescue medication now.
  • A first-ever unprovoked seizure — needs neuroimaging, labs, and an EEG; most warrant same-day ED evaluation.
  • Failure to return to baseline mental status >20–30 min after a seizure — assume non-convulsive SE until an EEG says otherwise.
  • Fever, headache, neck stiffness, or immunosuppression with a seizure — CNS infection. Needs LP ± empiric acyclovir and antibiotics now.
  • A new focal neurological deficit that does not resolve — stroke, mass, or encephalitis. Todd's paralysis is a diagnosis of exclusion, made after imaging, not before it.
  • Head trauma with the seizure, or a seizure that caused significant injury.
  • A seizure in pregnancy — eclampsia until proven otherwise.
  • A seizure cluster that has not responded to the home rescue dose.
  • Suspected drug toxicity or overdose — especially isoniazid, TCAs, bupropion, cocaine/sympathomimetics, theophylline.
  • Hypoglycemia, severe hyponatremia, or another severe metabolic derangement as the driver.
If you are on the phone with a family and a seizure is happening right now: tell them to look at a clock, give the rescue medication at 5 minutes, and call 911. Do not spend the call taking a history.
🛏️ Wards — the patient who seized, and the clock that is still running
Admit

Who gets admitted

📋

Admission criteria — and who can safely go home from the ED

Anyone who has genuinely been in status epilepticus is admitted. Full stop. The question on the wards is more often: this person had a seizure — do they stay?

Admit

  • Any episode meeting SE criteria (≥5 min, or recurrent without recovery) — even if it has now stopped.
  • Persistently altered mental status that has not returned to baseline.
  • A first-ever unprovoked seizure with an abnormal exam, abnormal imaging, or an incomplete workup.
  • A structural or symptomatic cause found: stroke, hemorrhage, tumour, abscess, encephalitis, TBI.
  • A metabolic cause that needs correction: severe hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, uremia.
  • Suspected CNS infection — needs LP and empiric therapy.
  • Alcohol/benzodiazepine/barbiturate withdrawal seizures — these cluster and escalate.
  • Seizure clusters / breakthrough seizures not controlled in the ED.
  • Significant injury, aspiration, rhabdomyolysis, or arrhythmia.
  • Pregnancy with a seizure.
  • Poor social support / no reliable observer and a meaningful recurrence risk.

Consider discharge from the ED

  • A known epileptic with a typical, brief, single seizure;
  • who has returned fully to baseline;
  • with an identified, correctable precipitant (a missed dose, sleep deprivation, an intercurrent illness);
  • a normal exam and a normal metabolic panel;
  • no injury;
  • a reliable adult at home and a plan;
  • a rescue medication in hand and outpatient neurology follow-up arranged;
  • and driving restrictions explicitly counselled and documented.

If you cannot check every one of those boxes, they stay.

"He's just post-ictal" is the most dangerous sentence on the wards. The post-ictal state should be improving, visibly, over 20–30 minutes. A patient whose mental status is flat or worsening is not post-ictal — they are still seizing, or they have a new structural lesion. Get an EEG and re-image.
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

Labs, imaging, monitoring — and exactly when

Structure mirrors NCS 2012 Table 3 ("Suggested diagnostic work-up"): the work-up runs simultaneously and in parallel with treatment — you never stop treating in order to investigate.

Every patient — immediately

Fingerstick glucoseFIRST. Before anything else. Hypoglycemia is a cause of SE that no ASM will fix and every minute of it kills neurons. This is the one test whose delay is indefensible.0–2 min
Thiamine 100 mg IV, then D50 if glucose <60Thiamine goes in BEFORE the glucose in anyone with alcohol use, malnutrition, hyperemesis, or bariatric surgery — a glucose load into a thiamine-deficient brain can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy.Immediate
Vitals + continuous cardiac monitor + pulse oximetryContinuously. Watch for the Phase 1 → Phase 2 transition: a falling blood pressure in SE is a late and ominous sign.Continuous
CBC, BMP, Mg, Ca (total & ionized), PhosEvery patient. Finds the correctable causes: hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, uremia, hypoglycemia.Immediate
ASM levelsIn anyone on an ASM. Sub-therapeutic levels are the single most common precipitant of SE in known epilepsy. Send a free phenytoin if the albumin is low.Immediate
LFTs, coags, CK, lactate, VBG/ABGCK for rhabdomyolysis (may be normal early — recheck at 12–24 h). Lactate is usually high and will normalize within ~1 h of seizure control. LFTs before valproate.Immediate
β-hCGAny person of childbearing potential. Changes both the differential (eclampsia) and the drug you may use.Immediate
Toxicology screen (urine + serum), ethanol levelWhen no clear cause. Specifically ask about the seizure-causing toxins: isoniazid, TCAs, bupropion, theophylline, cocaine and sympathomimetics, organophosphates, cyclosporine.If unclear
Non-contrast head CTAppropriate for most cases (NCS 2012). Rules out hemorrhage, mass, and herniation — the things that change what you do in the next 20 minutes. Do it once the patient is stable enough to travel.Immediate
Continuous EEG (cEEG)NCS 2012: initiate within 1 hour of suspected SE. Mandatory if the patient does not wake up after the convulsions stop. See the EEG module below.<1 h

Selected patients — based on the clinical picture

Lumbar punctureAny fever, headache, meningismus, immunosuppression, or unexplained SE. Get the CT first if there is focal deficit, papilledema, or depressed consciousness. Do NOT delay antibiotics/acyclovir for the LP — draw cultures and treat. Note that a seizure itself can cause a mild CSF pleocytosis, but you may never attribute pleocytosis to a seizure until infection is excluded.If suspicion
Empiric acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h ± antibioticsStart immediately if HSV encephalitis or bacterial meningitis is even plausible — fever, confusion, CSF pleocytosis, temporal lobe changes. The cost of a few days of acyclovir is trivial; the cost of missing HSV is not.Empiric
MRI brain with & without contrastWhen the CT is unrevealing and the cause is unclear; when the seizure was focal; for suspected encephalitis, autoimmune disease, PRES, or mesial temporal sclerosis. Far more sensitive than CT for everything that actually causes new SE.If unclear
Autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis panel (serum + CSF)Any new-onset refractory SE (NORSE) without a clear cause — anti-NMDA-R, LGI1, CASPR2, GAD65, and the paraneoplastic panel. Send it early: results take days, and if you wait for them to be positive before considering immunotherapy, you have already lost the window.NORSE
Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) 100 mg IVThe antidote in isoniazid overdose — give gram-for-gram with the ingested INH dose (or 5 g empirically if the amount is unknown). Also for pyridoxine-dependent seizures in young children. INH-induced SE will not stop until you give it.Antidote
Magnesium sulfate 4–6 g IV over 15–20 min, then 1–2 g/hEclampsia — magnesium is superior to phenytoin here. And delivering the fetus is the definitive treatment.Antidote
Troponin + ECGProlonged SE causes catecholamine-mediated myocardial injury, Takotsubo, and arrhythmia. Also gets your baseline QT/PR before lacosamide or fosphenytoin.If prolonged
Chest X-rayAspiration is common. Also finds neurogenic pulmonary edema.Common
ProlactinLargely unhelpful — know why. It rises after a GTC seizure but must be drawn 10–20 min after the event with a baseline for comparison, is useless beyond ~6 h, does not reliably rise after focal or non-convulsive seizures, and a normal value never excludes a seizure. Do not build a diagnosis on it, and do not let a normal prolactin talk you out of treating SE.Low yield
Treat

Acute management — the ladder, with real doses

💊

Stepwise therapy by the clock (AES 2016 · NCS 2012 · ESETT)

Before you read another word: the #1 error is benzodiazepine underdosing. The reflexive "lorazepam 2 mg IV" for an 80 kg adult is half the correct dose. Give 0.1 mg/kg — capped at 4 mg per dose — and be prepared to repeat it once. NCS 2012 links inadequate therapy (insufficient dose, wrong route, delays between treatments, no EEG) to mortality as high as 45%, versus 8% with adequate therapy. You do more harm by being timid here than by being aggressive.
1
0–5 min — Stabilize (and start the clock)
The things that are more important than the anticonvulsant
▾
  • Airway, breathing, circulation. Head positioning, jaw thrust, nasal/oral airway, high-flow O₂ (non-rebreather). Suction.
  • Note the time the seizure started. Everything downstream is indexed to it.
  • Fingerstick glucose. Immediately.
  • Thiamine 100 mg IV → then D50 50 mL IV if glucose <60 mg/dL. Thiamine first in the at-risk.
  • Two large-bore IVs, continuous cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, BP cuff.
  • Do not wait for IV access to give a benzodiazepine. If there is no IV at 5 minutes, give IM midazolam — RAMPART showed that a drug in the muscle now beats a drug in a vein later.
The stabilization phase is not a preamble — hypoxia, hypoglycemia, and hypotension each independently perpetuate the seizure and amplify the neuronal injury. You are removing the fuel while you reach for the extinguisher.
2
5–20 min — Benzodiazepine (FIRST-LINE, AES Level A)
Full dose. Repeat once. Then move on.
▾
Benzodiazepines are GABA-A positive allosteric modulators — they increase the frequency of chloride-channel opening, restoring the inhibition that is failing. Their efficacy is decaying by the minute as GABA-A receptors are internalized. This is a use-it-or-lose-it drug class.
DrugStart (dose)RateRepeatCeilingNotes / if unavailable
Lorazepam
IV drug of choice		 0.1 mg/kg IV
up to 4 mg per dose		 ≤ 2 mg/min IVP May repeat once in 5–10 min ≈8 mg total in an adult Dilute 1:1 with saline. Contains propylene glycol. AES Level A. Longer CNS duration than diazepam (less redistribution) — which is why it beats diazepam for SE.
Midazolam
IM drug of choice — when there is no IV		 10 mg IM if ≥40 kg
5 mg IM if 13–40 kg
(0.2 mg/kg IM, max 10 mg)		 Single IM injection Single dose (as studied in RAMPART) 10 mg AES Level A — and SUPERIOR to IV lorazepam when there is no IV access. RAMPART: seizure stopped before ED arrival in 73.4% vs 63.4%. The IM needle goes in at 1.2 min; the IV takes 4.8. Also: intranasal 0.2 mg/kg, buccal 0.5 mg/kg.
Diazepam 0.15–0.2 mg/kg IV
up to 10 mg per dose		 ≤ 5 mg/min IVP May repeat once in 5 min 2 doses AES Level A. Rapidly redistributes out of the brain (short CNS duration) — so it must be followed promptly by a longer-acting ASM. Rectal: 0.2–0.5 mg/kg.
Phenobarbital 15 mg/kg IV 50–100 mg/min — — An AES Level A initial-therapy alternative if none of the three benzodiazepines above is available. Not the routine first choice — profound sedation, respiratory depression, hypotension.
AES 2016 is explicit: do not give the initial therapy more than twice. Only IV lorazepam and IV diazepam may be repeated (once, at full dose). If two adequate benzodiazepine doses have not worked, the answer is not a third benzodiazepine — the receptors are gone. Move to the second-line agent immediately.
3
20–40 min — Established SE: the second-line ASM
ESETT: levetiracetam = fosphenytoin = valproate. Pick on the patient, not the drug.
▾

ESETT (Kapur, NEJM 2019) is one of the most practice-simplifying trials in neurology. 384 patients with benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive SE, randomized blind to one of three agents. The primary outcome — seizure cessation and improved consciousness by 60 min, without additional drug — was met in:

AgentSuccessLife-threatening hypotensionIntubation by 60 minDeath
Levetiracetam47% (95% CrI 39–55)0.7%20.0%4.7%
Fosphenytoin45% (95% CrI 36–54)3.2%26.4%2.4%
Valproate46% (95% CrI 38–55)1.6%16.8%1.6%

The trial was stopped for futility — there was a 1% probability of ever finding a winner. The three drugs are interchangeable in efficacy. Two consequences follow, and they are the whole point:

  1. You should choose the second-line agent on the patient's comorbidities, not on tradition. Hypotensive or bradyarrhythmic → not fosphenytoin. Liver disease or pregnancy or possible POLG → not valproate. Severe renal failure → dose-adjust levetiracetam. There is no efficacy price for choosing the safe one.
  2. Roughly half of patients will NOT respond. Have the refractory-SE plan (intubation, cEEG, an anesthetic infusion) queued up before you need it — do not start thinking about it at minute 40.
DrugDoseRate / infusion timeAdditional doseWhy it worksAvoid / watch
Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV
max 4500 mg		 Over 10–15 min (NCS: 2–5 mg/kg/min) — SV2A modulation → reduced presynaptic vesicle release. No hepatic metabolism, essentially no interactions, no hypotension. The safest choice in the hemodynamically fragile, the liver patient, and the pregnant patient. Renal dose-adjust for maintenance (not for the load). Somnolence, agitation.
Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV
max 1500 mg PE		 ≤ 150 mg PE/min May give an additional 5 mg/kg (NCS 2012) Use-dependent block of fast Na⁺-channel inactivation — preferentially silences rapidly firing neurons. Independent of GABA, so unaffected by receptor internalization. Hypotension and arrhythmia (rate-related) — needs cardiac monitoring. Highest intubation rate in ESETT (26.4%). Never in generalized/myoclonic epilepsy (worsens it). Fosphenytoin is a prodrug — dosed in "phenytoin equivalents," and it avoids the purple-glove syndrome and propylene glycol toxicity of IV phenytoin.
Valproate 40 mg/kg IV
max 3000 mg		 Over 10 min (NCS: 3–6 mg/kg/min) May give an additional 20 mg/kg (NCS 2012) Multi-target: Na⁺ + T-type Ca²⁺ channels + increased GABA. The best second-line agent in generalized, myoclonic, and absence SE. CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy, liver disease, and POLG/mitochondrial disease (fatal hepatotoxicity). Hyperammonemia, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia. Lowest intubation rate in ESETT (16.8%). Use with caution in TBI.
Phenytoin
(if no fosphenytoin)		 20 mg/kg IV ≤ 50 mg/min (much slower than fosphenytoin) Additional 5–10 mg/kg Same Na⁺-channel mechanism as fosphenytoin. Only compatible with saline (precipitates in dextrose). Propylene glycol diluent → hypotension and arrhythmia. Purple glove syndrome and tissue necrosis on extravasation. Fosphenytoin is preferred wherever it exists.
Phenobarbital 15–20 mg/kg IV 50–100 mg/min Additional 5–10 mg/kg GABA-A — prolongs the duration of channel opening, and at high concentration can open the channel without GABA. This is why it can work when benzodiazepines have failed. Profound sedation, respiratory depression, hypotension. Expect to intubate. A very reasonable second-line choice where valproate and levetiracetam are unavailable.
Lacosamide
(off-label; widely used)		 200–400 mg IV 200 mg over 15 min — Enhances SLOW Na⁺-channel inactivation — a different mechanism from fosphenytoin, so it can be added to it. Listed in NCS 2012 (Class IIb, Level C) — the evidence base is thinner than for the ESETT three. PR prolongation — avoid in 2nd/3rd-degree AV block. A good add-on when you have already used one Na⁺ blocker and need another lever.
Which second-line agent, in which patient?
  • Hypotensive, bradycardic, in heart block, or on the edge of needing pressors → levetiracetam (lowest hypotension rate) or valproate. Not fosphenytoin.
  • Cirrhosis / hepatic failure → levetiracetam. Not valproate.
  • Pregnant → levetiracetam or fosphenytoin (NCS 2012). Not valproate. And consider eclampsia → magnesium.
  • Known generalized / myoclonic / absence epilepsy → valproate. Not fosphenytoin (it can worsen these).
  • Severe renal failure → any of the three; adjust levetiracetam maintenance (the load is unchanged).
  • Already on one of them at home with a sub-therapeutic level → re-load that same drug. NCS 2012 explicitly endorses this: bolus the drug they were already on.
  • Suspected POLG / mitochondrial disease → anything except valproate.
4
>40 min — Refractory SE: this is now an ICU problem
Failed a benzo + one ASM = RSE. Call the unit; do not run a third bolus and hope.
▾

Refractory SE (NCS 2012) = SE that does not respond to the standard regimen — a benzodiazepine plus one second-line ASM. That is the definition, and by that definition roughly half of ESETT patients were refractory at 60 minutes. It is not a rare, exotic endpoint; it is the expected outcome in a substantial minority of the patients in front of you.

NCS 2012 is unambiguous about what to do: "There is no well defined period of observation that has been determined to be safe, and no data to suggest that watchful waiting is safer than proceeding with more aggressive treatment. Hence, we recommend proceeding with additional treatment immediately."

  • Call the ICU and neurology now.
  • Intubate — you are about to give an anesthetic infusion.
  • Get continuous EEG on — from this point on the seizure is largely invisible, and cEEG is the only way to know whether treatment is working.
  • Start a continuous IV anesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol, or pentobarbital). Full dosing in the ICU panel.
  • If the patient is hemodynamically stable, not intubated, and has non-convulsive SE, NCS 2012 does allow considering an additional bolus ASM (valproate, levetiracetam, or fosphenytoin, if not already given) rather than going straight to anesthesia. That latitude does not exist for convulsive SE.
Do not park a refractory SE patient on the floor. A patient who has failed a benzodiazepine and a second-line agent needs an airway, an anesthetic infusion, and an EEG — none of which the floor can provide. The hours spent "watching" are the hours in which the hippocampus dies.

After the seizure stops: converting the load into maintenance

Stopping the seizure is half the job. Every patient who required a load needs maintenance ASM therapy started, or the seizure simply comes back. NCS 2012: all patients presenting with SE need emergent initial therapy AND urgent control therapy in addition to AED maintenance therapy, even if SE is immediately controlled.

Drug loadedMaintenance doseStart whenTarget levelNotes
Levetiracetam1000–1500 mg IV/PO q12h (max 3000 mg/day)12 h after the loadNo standard rangeRenally adjust (CrCl 30–50 → 250–750 q12h; <30 → 250–500 q12h; ESRD → 500–1000 q24h + 250–500 after HD). IV:PO is 1:1.
Fosphenytoin / phenytoin4–6 mg/kg/day divided q8–12h (≈100 mg q8h in a typical adult)12 h after the load10–20 µg/mL total; 1–2 freeZero-order kinetics — check a level before adjusting. Send a free level if albumin is low.
Valproate10–15 mg/kg/day divided q6–12h (titrate up)6–12 h after the load50–100 µg/mLWatch ammonia, platelets, LFTs, lipase.
Lacosamide100–200 mg IV/PO q12h12 h after the loadNo standard rangeECG for PR interval. IV:PO 1:1.
Phenobarbital1–3 mg/kg/day (typically 60–120 mg/day)12–24 h after the load15–40 µg/mLHalf-life ~4 days — steady state takes weeks; do not chase early levels.
If they were on an ASM at home and the level was low, the answer is usually to reload and continue THAT drug — not to add a new one. The drug wasn't failing; the patient wasn't taking it. Adding a second agent to a regimen that was never actually being taken just creates two drugs they will not take.
Calculate

Weight-based dose calculator

🧮

Status epilepticus dose ladder — enter the weight

AES 2016 · NCS 2012 · ESETT

The commonest error in this disease is arithmetic under pressure. Enter the weight and read the doses — including the caps, which are where people go wrong in both directions (giving 8 mg of lorazepam as a single dose, or giving 2 mg to a 90 kg adult).

Doses per AES 2016 (Glauser), NCS 2012 (Brophy, Tables 7–8) and ESETT (Kapur, NEJM 2019). Always confirm against your institution's protocol and the patient's comorbidities — this tool does the multiplication, not the thinking. It does not adjust for renal or hepatic impairment.

📊

Prognostic scores — and why there is no calculator here

The 2026 NCS/DGNI neuroprognostication guideline reviewed every prognostic variable and model in status epilepticus and concluded, verbatim: "None of the variables and models selected were identified as reliable predictors of mortality in patients with SE." That includes STESS, mSTESS, and EMSE — and also age, comorbidity index, etiology, seizure type, level of consciousness, SE duration, and even the development of refractory or super-refractory SE. There is no score that tells you this patient will die. This is the most important thing on this page, and it is why no prognostic calculator is built into this guide.

Two scores are nonetheless widely quoted, and you will be asked about them. Here is what they are, what they are worth, and why they are linked out rather than reimplemented.

ScoreWhat it usesPerformance (2026 NCS systematic review)Why there is no live calculator here
STESS
Status Epilepticus Severity Score		 Four variables, assessed before treatment: level of consciousness, worst seizure type, age, and history of previous seizures. Total 0–6. AUC 0.63–0.84. PPV only 27–33% at a cut-off of 3; NPV 85–95%. The optimal cut-off (3 vs 4) remains genuinely unsettled. Graded "not reliable" for counseling an individual patient. Two reasons. First, the exact per-option point values could not be verified from an accessible primary or MDCalc source, and we do not guess at arithmetic that drives a prognostic estimate. Second — and more importantly — a score with a 27–33% PPV should not be handed to you as a confident-looking number in a box. → STESS on MDCalc
EMSE
Epidemiology-based Mortality Score in SE		 Weighted points across etiology, age, comorbidity (Charlson), and EEG; some versions add duration and consciousness. Derivation AUC ~0.9 — but not reproduced: validation AUCs 0.69–0.86, and the optimal cut-off is uncertain. The 2026 guideline found "insufficient evidence to support the use of the EMSE in counseling surrogates." The exact point allocations are not verifiable from an accessible primary source. Link out rather than approximate. → Leitinger et al., Neurocrit Care 2015

What the 2026 guideline says to do INSTEAD

  1. Establish the goals of care with the surrogate first — ranging from seizure control to functional independence — and prognosticate against those goals, not against a score.
  2. Tell families the truth about the timeline. Verbatim: "prolonged sedative infusions and long-acting antiseizure medications may result in prolonged coma and dependence on life-sustaining measures … for a variable duration ranging from days to months." Set that expectation on day 1, not day 20.
  3. Say explicitly that recovery is possible. Verbatim: "a long-term recovery that reaches or approximates the patient's baseline level of functioning is feasible" — even in refractory and super-refractory SE.
  4. Prognosticate only in the absence of confounders. Delay it when there is residual sedation, a toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, or a prolonged post-ictal state. Defer entirely when the etiology is unclear.
  5. Use etiology-specific validated tools where they exist (e.g. the multimodal post-cardiac-arrest pathway) — because etiology is the variable that actually carries the prognosis.
Put the two guidelines together and the message is unmistakable. NCS 2012: patients treated for refractory SE for weeks to months can still recover fully, and the duration of anesthetic treatment "does not appear to be indicative of long term prognosis." NCS/DGNI 2026: no variable or model reliably predicts a poor outcome. So do not use a high STESS, a long ICU course, or the sheer number of failed drugs to justify withdrawing care. Find the etiology, treat it, remove the confounders, wait for the drugs to clear — and only then prognosticate.
EEG

Continuous EEG — who, when, how long

📉

The test that finds the seizure you cannot see

After convulsive SE stops, a substantial fraction of patients keep seizing electrically. In the landmark work on this, roughly half of patients whose convulsions had been controlled had ongoing electrographic seizures, and about 14% were in frank non-convulsive status epilepticus. These patients look "post-ictal." They are not. They are being injured, invisibly, while you round on someone else.

Indication for cEEGWhyDuration
Persistently altered mental status after convulsive SE (not waking up within 20–30 min)The single strongest indication. This is how NCSE is found.≥24 h; at least 48 h if comatose
Any patient on a continuous anesthetic infusion for RSEMandatory. The infusion is titrated to the EEG. Without it you are dosing blind. NCS 2012: "cEEG findings, not serum drug levels, guide therapy."Throughout, plus 24 h after seizures stop and during every weaning trial
Any patient who is pharmacologically paralyzedA neuromuscular blocker abolishes the motor signs but not the seizure. A paralyzed patient without EEG is a total blind spot.Continuous
Unexplained coma or encephalopathyNon-convulsive seizures are common in comatose patients with TBI, ICH, SAH, sepsis, cardiac arrest, and CNS infection.48 h if comatose (NCS 2012)
Post-cardiac-arrestBoth to detect NCSE and to prognosticate (myoclonic status, burst-suppression, absent reactivity).≥24–48 h
Subtle or fluctuating motor phenomena — nystagmus, eye deviation, facial or finger twitching"Subtle SE" — electromechanical dissociation. This is what late convulsive SE decays into.≥24 h
NCS 2012 timing, exactly: cEEG should be initiated within 1 HOUR of suspected SE onset if seizures are ongoing. Duration: at least 48 hours in comatose patients after an acute brain insult, and 24 hours after electrographic seizures stop or during weaning trials of the anesthetic.
The single most impactful order you can write on a floor patient who "isn't waking up" after a seizure is an EEG. The differential — post-ictal state, NCSE, a new stroke, over-sedation, metabolic encephalopathy — has exactly one member you can neither see nor treat without the EEG, and it is the one that is actively causing further brain injury.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend every single day

WhatTarget / what you're looking forWhy it matters
Mental status — a documented, structured neuro examSteadily improving. Anything else is a failure of the treatment plan.The most important variable on the list. A plateau or decline = EEG + re-image. Do not accept "unchanged" for two days running.
Seizure count / event logZero clinical seizuresAny recurrence means the maintenance regimen is inadequate. Nursing should document every event with the time.
EEG (if on cEEG)No electrographic seizures; background improving/reactiveThe only objective measure of whether you have won. Read the report every day.
ASM levelPhenytoin 10–20 (free 1–2); valproate 50–100; phenobarbital 15–40Confirms you are actually therapeutic. Send a free phenytoin if albumin is low.
BMP + Mg + Phos + CaNa⁺ normal; Mg >2; Phos and Ca normalCorrecting these is treating the seizure. Hyponatremia and hypomagnesemia in particular.
CKFalling. Recheck at 12–24 h even if the first was normal.Rhabdomyolysis peaks late. CK >5000 → aggressive IV fluids to protect the kidneys.
Creatinine + urine outputUOP >0.5 mL/kg/h; creatinine stableMyoglobin-induced AKI. Tea-coloured urine with a positive dipstick for blood but no red cells on microscopy = myoglobinuria.
LactateShould normalize within ~1 h of seizure control.A lactate that does NOT clear is a different problem — sepsis, ischemic bowel, ongoing (non-convulsive) seizure. That is a genuinely useful signal.
TemperatureNormothermiaHyperthermia worsens neuronal injury. And a fever might be the infection that caused the whole thing — reassess, don't just assume it's the seizure.
Aspiration / respiratory statusClear chest, adequate cough, SpO₂ >92%Aspiration pneumonitis and pneumonia are the commonest medical complications after convulsive SE.
LFTs, ammonia, platelets, lipase (if on valproate)NormalValproate causes hyperammonemic encephalopathy with a normal LFT panel and a therapeutic level. If a valproate patient isn't waking up, check an ammonia before you blame the seizure.
DVT prophylaxis, aspiration precautions, mobility, delirium screenAll activeThe boring stuff that determines whether they leave with a functional life.
The lactate is a gift. A post-seizure lactate of 9 that is 2 an hour later tells you the seizure has genuinely stopped and you are not septic. A post-seizure lactate of 9 that is still 8 four hours later tells you something else is going on — and it is usually either an ongoing non-convulsive seizure or a second diagnosis you have not made.
Escalate

When to call the ICU

⬆️

Numeric escalation triggers — no hand-waving

Transfer to ICU for ANY of the following:
  • Refractory SE — seizure persists after an adequate benzodiazepine plus one second-line ASM. This alone is the trigger, and it is non-negotiable: RSE requires intubation, an anesthetic infusion, and cEEG.
  • Seizure duration >40–60 min despite treatment. NCS 2012: definitive control should be established within 60 minutes of onset.
  • Any need for a continuous IV anesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol, pentobarbital, ketamine).
  • Airway compromise: inability to protect the airway; GCS ≤8; SpO₂ <90% on high-flow O₂; PaCO₂ rising; a respiratory rate that is failing.
  • Hemodynamic instability: SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <70 mmHg (NCS 2012 threshold for starting vasopressor support), or a new need for vasopressors after fosphenytoin/phenobarbital.
  • Non-convulsive SE on EEG requiring aggressive treatment.
  • Any pharmacologic paralysis — a paralyzed patient must be on cEEG in an ICU.
  • Serious arrhythmia — including new bradycardia or heart block after fosphenytoin or lacosamide.
  • Severe metabolic derangement: pH <7.2 that is not clearing after seizure control; K⁺ >6.0; CK >5000 with rising creatinine or oliguria.
  • Temperature >40 °C, or evidence of neurogenic pulmonary edema.
  • The underlying cause needs the unit anyway — herniation, large stroke, meningitis/encephalitis with depressed consciousness, eclampsia, severe toxidrome.
The hidden escalation trigger: the patient who is not waking up. A patient whose convulsions stopped 90 minutes ago and who is still unresponsive is, until an EEG says otherwise, in non-convulsive status epilepticus — and that is an ICU problem, not a "let's reassess in the morning" problem. This is the escalation that gets missed, because nothing on the monitor is alarming.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness — and where they actually go

Discharge readiness — all of these, not most of them

  • Seizure-free for ≥24 h (clinically, and on EEG if they were on cEEG).
  • Mental status back at, or reliably trending to, baseline.
  • The cause has been identified and addressed — or a definite plan exists to complete the workup as an outpatient.
  • On a stable maintenance ASM regimen, taking it by mouth, with a therapeutic level where one applies.
  • Metabolic derangements corrected; CK falling; renal function stable.
  • Swallowing assessed (aspiration risk is high after SE) and nutrition established.
  • A RESCUE MEDICATION prescribed, and the caregiver taught how to use it. Do not discharge an SE survivor without one. This is the intervention that prevents the readmission.
  • A written seizure action plan in hand.
  • Driving restriction counselled and documented.
  • Neurology follow-up arranged — with a date, not a phone number.
  • Precipitant addressed: if it was non-adherence, the reason for it has actually been fixed (cost, access, side effects, cognition, housing) — not just re-prescribed.

Home

Back to baseline, independent, reliable caregiver, rescue med in hand, follow-up booked. The precipitant is understood and fixed.

Home health

Home, but needs skilled nursing visits (med teaching, ASM titration, wound care) or in-home PT/OT. Good for the older patient with a mild new deficit.

SNF

Needs 24 h skilled nursing but cannot tolerate ≥3 h/day of therapy. The typical route for a deconditioned elderly patient after prolonged SE.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3 h/day of therapy across ≥2 disciplines and has clear rehab potential. The right call for a younger patient with a post-SE or post-stroke deficit.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care — ventilator weaning after a long anesthetic run, tracheostomy, complex wounds. Expected stay >25 days.

Hospice / palliative

Devastating anoxic brain injury, end-stage disease, or goals of care that have shifted to comfort. Involve palliative care EARLY in the super-refractory and post-arrest patient — not as a last resort at week three.
The disposition decision that most often gets made wrong is the anoxic-brain-injury patient. Post-cardiac-arrest myoclonic status has a poor but not uniformly hopeless prognosis, and prognostication must be multimodal and delayed — exam off sedation, EEG reactivity, SSEPs, NSE, and MRI — not a single EEG pattern on day 1. Do not prognosticate on a sedated patient. Give it time, gather the data, and involve palliative care in parallel rather than instead.
🫀 ICU — refractory & super-refractory status epilepticus
Admit

ICU triggers & severity

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

The line is bright: refractory status epilepticus is an ICU disease. RSE means the seizure has survived an adequate benzodiazepine and one second-line ASM — which means it needs a drug that will stop the patient breathing, an EEG to know whether that drug is working, and a vasopressor for the blood pressure it will drop. None of those things live on the floor.

StageTriggerWhat the ICU addsMortality
Refractory SE (RSE)Fails a benzodiazepine + one second-line ASM (NCS 2012). In ESETT, ~53% of patients did not respond to the second-line agent — this is common, not exotic.Intubation, continuous anesthetic infusion, cEEG, arterial line, vasopressors.23–61% at discharge
Super-refractory SE (SRSE)SE that continues or recurs ≥24 h after starting IV anesthesia — including recurrence on weaning the anesthetic.Ketamine, add-on ASMs, immunotherapy, ketogenic diet, inhaled anesthetics, and a long conversation about goals.~30–50% long-term
NORSE / FIRESNew-onset RSE in a patient without epilepsy and with no clear structural/toxic/metabolic cause (NORSE); preceded by a febrile illness 2 weeks–24 h before onset (FIRES).Aggressive autoimmune workup + EARLY empiric immunotherapy. Do not wait for antibody results.High
NCSE in the comatose ICU patientElectrographic SE without convulsions — found only on cEEG.The EEG itself. Treatment intensity is calibrated to the clinical context (see below).18–52% at discharge
ICU admission is triggered by any of: refractory SE · need for any continuous anesthetic infusion · need for intubation or airway compromise (GCS ≤8) · SBP <90 or MAP <70 (NCS 2012 threshold for vasopressor support) · pharmacologic paralysis · NCSE requiring aggressive treatment · seizure duration >60 min despite treatment · serious arrhythmia · CK >5000 with AKI · a cause that needs the unit anyway (herniation, meningitis, eclampsia, cardiac arrest).
Not all non-convulsive SE deserves a barbiturate coma. There is a real and important distinction between the ambulatory, "wandering confused" NCSE patient — who often does well and should NOT be intubated and anesthetized — and the comatose, critically-ill NCSE patient after convulsive SE, who should be treated aggressively. Treating the first like the second causes iatrogenic harm: you will intubate someone who was walking, and give them a ventilator-associated pneumonia. Match the aggression of the treatment to the aggression of the disease.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, leads, and what you are titrating to

Continuous EEGThe single non-negotiable monitor. The infusion is titrated to the EEG, not to the exam and not to a drug level — NCS 2012: "cEEG findings, not serum drug levels, guide therapy." Once you start an anesthetic, the patient's motor signs are gone; the EEG is your only window. Start within 1 h.Mandatory
Arterial lineBefore or immediately after starting the anesthetic. Every one of these drugs causes hypotension, and you will be titrating both the anesthetic and a vasopressor against each other, minute by minute.Standard
Central venous accessVasopressors, high-concentration infusions, and the reality that this patient will be here for days. Pentobarbital in particular will require pressors.Standard
Endotracheal tube + ventilatorAssumed. Every continuous anesthetic infusion requires mechanical ventilation.Mandatory
Foley catheterNCS 2012 lists it in the critical-care bundle: you need accurate urine output to track myoglobinuric AKI and volume status.Standard
Core temperatureContinuous. Hyperthermia worsens neuronal injury; and pentobarbital abolishes shivering and thermoregulation.Standard
Labs: CK, K⁺, creatinine, lactate, ABG, LFTs, triglyceridesCK and K⁺ for rhabdomyolysis. Triglycerides, lactate, CK, pH and the ECG are the propofol-infusion-syndrome surveillance panel — check them daily on any propofol run.Daily
ICP monitoringOnly if the underlying pathology warrants it (large stroke, TBI, fulminant hepatic failure) — not for SE per se.Selected

The EEG target — what "enough" looks like

NCS 2012 is refreshingly honest here: "There are currently no data to support a standardized regimen for the intensity and duration of treatment for RSE." What it does say is that the intensity is dictated by the cEEG, with the goal being either cessation of electrographic seizures OR burst-suppression.

Seizure suppression

Titrate only until electrographic seizures stop. Less drug, less hypotension, shorter ventilation, less ileus and immunosuppression. Reasonable for most patients, and the more common modern practice.

Burst-suppression

Titrate deeper, to a pattern of high-voltage bursts alternating with near-flat suppression (commonly targeting interburst intervals on the order of ~10–20 s, or a specified burst-suppression ratio). More drug, more hypotension, more pressor. Reserved for the seizure that will not stop at the lighter target. There is no high-quality evidence that burst-suppression beats seizure-suppression on outcome — it is a deeper target, not a proven better one.

PhaseWhat you doSource
AchieveTitrate the infusion until electrographic seizures stop (or burst-suppression is reached).NCS 2012
MaintainHold at that target for 24–48 hours.NCS 2012 — "customarily, electrographic seizure control is maintained for 24–48 h"
WeanGradual withdrawal of the infusion, on cEEG, over ~24 h. Make sure the maintenance ASMs are at therapeutic levels before you start weaning — the maintenance drug is what has to hold the line.NCS 2012
If it recurs on weaningGo back to the prior (or a higher) infusion rate for a further period, ± add another agent. Recurrence on weaning at ≥24 h = super-refractory SE by definition.NCS 2012
Treat

Continuous anesthetic infusions

💉

Load → infusion → titration → max (NCS 2012, Table 8)

The core of RSE therapy
Every drug in this table is a GABA-A drug except ketamine. That is the whole problem, and the whole insight. GABA-A drugs are fighting for a receptor pool that status epilepticus has been actively depleting — which is why they need anesthetic doses to do what 4 mg of lorazepam would have done at minute 5, and why ketamine, which attacks the receptor that has been accumulating, becomes more attractive the longer this goes on.

NCS 2012 is explicit that there are insufficient data to say whether midazolam, propofol, or pentobarbital is preferred. Choose on the patient:

AgentLoadInitial infusionTitration (breakthrough SE)Range / maxSerious adverse effects
Midazolam
Often first choice		 0.2 mg/kg IV, given at an infusion rate of 2 mg/min Start the continuous infusion at the low end and titrate up Breakthrough: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg bolus, and increase the infusion rate by 0.05–0.1 mg/kg/h every 3–4 h 0.05–2 mg/kg/h Respiratory depression, hypotension. Tachyphylaxis occurs with prolonged use — the dose that worked yesterday may not work today, and that is expected, not failure. Active metabolite is renally eliminated → accumulates in AKI, giving a prolonged wake-up. Does NOT contain propylene glycol (unlike lorazepam and pentobarbital) — and causes less hypotension than the barbiturates, which is why it is often the opening move.
Propofol 1–2 mg/kg IV loading dose Start at 20 mcg/kg/min Breakthrough: increase the rate by 5–10 mcg/kg/min every 5 min, or give a 1 mg/kg bolus plus rate titration 30–200 mcg/kg/min
Use caution at >80 mcg/kg/min for >48 h		 PROPOFOL INFUSION SYNDROME (PRIS) — the reason for that caution line. Hypotension (especially with the load in a critically ill patient), respiratory depression, cardiac failure, rhabdomyolysis, metabolic acidosis, renal failure. Must adjust the daily caloric intake — propofol carries 1.1 kcal/mL of lipid. Contraindicated in young children.
Pentobarbital
The heavy artillery		 5–15 mg/kg, may give an additional 5–10 mg/kg; administer at ≤50 mg/min Start the continuous infusion after the load Breakthrough: 5 mg/kg bolus, and increase the infusion rate by 0.5–1 mg/kg/h every 12 h 0.5–5 mg/kg/h Hypotension (expect to need pressors), cardiac depression, respiratory depression, paralytic ileus, immunosuppression. At high doses, complete loss of neurological function — the exam is gone, so the EEG is everything. Long context-sensitive half-time → a wake-up measured in days. IV contains propylene glycol (→ anion-gap acidosis, AKI; check an osmolar gap on prolonged runs). Prolonged infusions risk withdrawal seizures as levels fall.
Thiopental
(not available in the US)		 2–7 mg/kg at ≤50 mg/min Continuous infusion Breakthrough: 1–2 mg/kg bolus, increase rate by 0.5–1 mg/kg/h every 12 h 0.5–5 mg/kg/h As pentobarbital. Metabolized TO pentobarbital, so it accumulates and the effective duration is even longer.
Ketamine
NMDA antagonist		 1–3 mg/kg IV (some protocols to 5 mg/kg) Start the infusion and titrate to EEG Titrate up against the EEG; commonly used in addition to, not instead of, a GABA-ergic infusion Commonly 1–5 mg/kg/h; some protocols and reviews go to 7.5 mg/kg/h or higher in SRSE The hemodynamic advantage is the point: ketamine is sympathomimetic and does NOT drop the blood pressure — it is pressor-sparing, and often raises MAP. Listed in NCS 2012 as an emerging/alternative therapy for RSE. Reported seizure control in roughly half of RSE/SRSE cases in the observational literature (Gaspard's multicentre series and subsequent registries). Caution: raises ICP in theory (increasingly questioned); hypersalivation; emergence phenomena.
Which infusion, in which patient?
  • Default opening move → midazolam. Least hypotension of the GABA-ergic three, no propylene glycol, familiar, titratable. Its weakness is tachyphylaxis and renal accumulation.
  • Need rapid, precise titration and a fast neuro exam on the other side → propofol. Its weakness is PRIS and the lipid load. Watch the rate ceiling.
  • Nothing else is working → pentobarbital. It has the highest reported acute seizure-control rate — and the highest complication rate. You are trading brain for organs; make that trade deliberately, and expect pressors, ileus, and days of coma.
  • Hypotensive, or already on high-dose pressors → add KETAMINE. It is the only agent here that will not make the blood pressure worse, and it is mechanistically the right drug late in the disease.
  • AKI → midazolam accumulates (active renal metabolite). Expect a slow wake-up and do not mistake it for a poor neurological prognosis.
Load the maintenance ASMs to therapeutic levels while the infusion is running — not when you start weaning. The anesthetic is a bridge, not a treatment. When you take the bridge away, something has to be holding the patient up, and that something is a fully-loaded levetiracetam/valproate/fosphenytoin/lacosamide regimen at a real therapeutic level. Weaning an anesthetic off a half-loaded ASM regimen is how patients bounce straight back into SRSE.
Support

Pressors & hemodynamics

💗

The blood pressure you are about to destroy

The hypotension in refractory SE is almost entirely iatrogenic — you caused it with the anesthetic. It is not distributive shock, and it does not need a big fluid resuscitation. It is vasoplegia plus myocardial depression from a GABA-ergic anesthetic, and it responds to an α₁ agonist. Meanwhile, in Phase 2 of SE, cerebral autoregulation has failed and cerebral perfusion is now passively dependent on MAP — so letting the pressure drop is not a benign trade-off, it is a second brain insult layered onto the first.

NCS 2012 threshold: start vasopressor support if SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <70 mmHg, to support cerebral perfusion pressure.

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick it in SE
Norepinephrine α₁ >> β₁ 0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min (titrate to MAP); higher in refractory vasoplegia ↑↑ SVR, modest ↑ contractility, minimal chronotropy First-line. The anesthetic caused vasoplegia; norepinephrine reverses exactly that, with enough β₁ to offset the myocardial depression of propofol/pentobarbital.
Phenylephrine Pure α₁ 0.5–9 mcg/kg/min (or 20–200 mcg/min) ↑↑ SVR; reflex bradycardia; no inotropy When the patient is tachycardic and you want pressure without more chronotropy — e.g. after a big ketamine load, or in a patient with tachyarrhythmia.
Vasopressin V₁ receptor (non-catecholamine) 0.03 units/min fixed (not titrated) ↑ SVR via a catecholamine-independent pathway Catecholamine-sparing add-on when norepinephrine requirements climb. Works when the adrenergic receptors are down-regulated.
Epinephrine α₁ + β₁ + β₂ 0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min ↑ SVR, ↑↑ CO, ↑ HR; raises lactate (β₂-driven glycolysis) Rescue when norepinephrine + vasopressin are insufficient, or if there is significant myocardial depression. Its lactate effect will muddy the one lab that was actually telling you something useful.
Dobutamine β₁ > β₂ (inotrope, not a pressor) 2.5–10 mcg/kg/min ↑ CO, ↓ SVR — may LOWER the blood pressure Only for genuine cardiogenic depression (e.g. pentobarbital-induced myocardial failure with a low cardiac output), and always alongside a vasopressor.
When the pressor requirement is escalating, the answer is often to change the ANESTHETIC, not to add a fourth pressor. If you are climbing the norepinephrine ladder to keep the MAP up against a pentobarbital infusion, add ketamine — it will let you back off the GABA-ergic agent, and it raises blood pressure rather than lowering it. Two drips fighting each other is a bad plan; one drip that does both jobs is a better one.
Do not chase the lactate with bicarbonate. The profound lactic acidosis of convulsive SE is generated by muscle and clears on its own within roughly an hour of seizure control. Bicarbonate here treats a number, worsens intracellular acidosis, and distracts you. If the lactate is NOT clearing, that is a real signal — look for ongoing non-convulsive seizure, sepsis, bowel ischemia, or (on a propofol drip) PRIS.
Airway

Intubation & ventilation

🌬️

The paralytic decision — and the settings

DO NOT give a long-acting paralytic to a patient in status epilepticus unless they are on continuous EEG. A neuromuscular blocker abolishes the convulsion but does nothing whatsoever to the seizure. You will have created a patient who looks treated, is being injured continuously, and has no observable sign left to tell you. If you must paralyze for intubation, use a short-acting agent (succinylcholine, or rocuronium if succinylcholine is contraindicated) — and get the EEG on immediately. If a patient is paralyzed, cEEG is mandatory, not optional.

A note on succinylcholine: it is the shortest-acting option and therefore preferred here, but avoid it if there is established rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalemia (a real risk after prolonged convulsive SE), or in known neuromuscular disease. In that setting use rocuronium — and accept that you have now blinded yourself for 30–60 minutes, which makes the EEG even more urgent.

Induction — pick an agent that treats the disease

You have to give an induction agent anyway. Choose one that is also an anticonvulsant. This is a free win that is routinely squandered.

Induction agentDoseEffect on the seizureVerdict
Propofol1–2 mg/kg IVAnticonvulsant (GABA-A) — and you were probably going to start it as an infusion anyway.✅ Excellent choice. Drops the BP; have a pressor ready.
Ketamine1–2 mg/kg IVAnticonvulsant (NMDA antagonist) — mechanistically ideal in late SE.✅ Excellent choice, especially if hypotensive. Preserves the blood pressure.
Midazolam0.2 mg/kg IVAnticonvulsant (GABA-A).✅ Good — doubles as your RSE load.
Etomidate0.3 mg/kg IVCan be PRO-convulsant — it produces myoclonus and activates epileptiform activity.⚠️ Avoid in SE if you have an alternative. Hemodynamically kind, but it is the wrong drug for this disease.

Initial ventilator settings

Mode
AC/VC
volume-control assist-control
Tidal volume
6–8 mL/kg IBW
lung-protective; aspiration is common
PEEP
5–8 cmH₂O
titrate to oxygenation
FiO₂

target SpO₂ 92–96%

NORMOCAPNIA — see below
