Target normocapnia — do not hyperventilate. It is tempting to hyperventilate a patient with a big lactic acidosis and a "brain problem." Resist it. Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and reduces cerebral blood flow — which is precisely the wrong thing to do to a brain that is metabolically maxed out and has already lost its autoregulation. Prophylactic hyperventilation is reserved for impending herniation, and nothing else.
The acidosis will fix itself. Post-SE metabolic acidosis with a lactate of 10 typically corrects within about an hour of seizure control, on its own. Do not hyperventilate to compensate, do not give bicarbonate, and do not let a scary-looking gas talk you into either. Treat the seizure; the gas follows.

Other ICU care that actually matters

  • Aggressive IV fluids if CK is rising — myoglobinuric AKI is preventable, and this is the window.
  • Aspiration precautions, early enteral nutrition (and remember to subtract propofol's 1.1 kcal/mL from the feeding prescription, or you will steadily overfeed and hypertriglyceridemia will follow).
  • DVT prophylaxis — these patients are immobile for days.
  • Stress-ulcer prophylaxis, per unit protocol.
  • Bowel regimen — pentobarbital causes paralytic ileus, reliably.
  • Eye care, pressure-area care, physiotherapy. A patient in a barbiturate coma cannot move, blink, or complain.
  • Daily temperature control — treat fever aggressively (hyperthermia worsens neuronal injury), but note that therapeutic hypothermia is not indicated (see below).
Rescue

Super-refractory SE — the rescue therapies

⚙️

When 24 hours of anesthesia hasn't worked

Super-refractory SE = SE that continues or recurs ≥24 h after starting IV anesthesia, including recurrence on weaning it. Roughly 10–15% of SE ends up here. The evidence base collapses at this point: NCS 2012's own table of alternative therapies for RSE is a list of case series, and it says so. Everything below is low-quality evidence. That is not a reason to do nothing — it is a reason to be honest with the family, to escalate in a structured order, and to think hard about etiology, because etiology is what determines whether any of it works.

Read this before you believe any SRSE case series — including the ones in the tables below. Allopregnanolone (SAGE-547) looked spectacular in its open-label series: 73% of patients weaned off anesthesia. Then it was tested against placebo in a randomized trial — and the PLACEBO arm weaned off anesthesia 42.4% of the time. The drug failed.

The lesson generalizes, and it is the single most important thing to understand about this entire section: a large fraction of super-refractory patients come off anesthesia eventually no matter what you do. Any uncontrolled case series — for ketamine, for the ketogenic diet, for ECT, for immunotherapy, for inhaled anesthetics — is therefore at serious risk of simply describing natural history and calling it a treatment effect. Reported "response rates" around 40–50% in an uncontrolled SRSE series are, on their own, indistinguishable from doing nothing.

This does not mean these therapies don't work — it means we genuinely do not know, and you should hold them with that uncertainty rather than with the false confidence of a percentage. It is also why the two interventions with a real mechanistic and outcome signal — immunotherapy in NORSE/FIRES, and surgery for a resectable focus — deserve priority over the rest of the list.

1
First: ketamine, and re-examine the diagnosis
The two highest-yield moves in SRSE
▾

Ketamine — load 1–3 mg/kg, infusion commonly 1–5 mg/kg/h (some protocols to 7.5 mg/kg/h). Add it to, rather than substitute it for, the GABA-ergic infusion. Two reasons it belongs here and not later:

  • It is the mechanistically correct drug. By 24 hours, GABA-A receptors have been internalized and NMDA receptors have been trafficked into the synapse. You are fighting a battle over a receptor that is disappearing, while ignoring one that is multiplying.
  • It is hemodynamically free. It is sympathomimetic — it lets you reduce the GABA-ergic infusion and the pressors at the same time. Observational series (Gaspard's multicentre cohort and subsequent registries) report seizure control in roughly half of RSE/SRSE cases.
And re-examine the diagnosis, hard. A seizure that will not stop after 24 hours of anesthesia is telling you that you have not found the cause. Go back and ask: is this autoimmune encephalitis? Is this HSV? Is this an ongoing toxidrome (INH — give pyridoxine)? Is this PNES that has been intubated? Is this a POLG patient I have been giving valproate to? Is there an unresected structural lesion? The most valuable thing in SRSE is usually a diagnosis, not another drug.
2
Load additional anti-seizure medications
Cheap, safe, and often forgotten while everyone stares at the drips
▾

The anesthetic is a bridge. Maximize the ASMs underneath it — these are what will hold the patient when you wean.

DrugDoseWhy here
Lacosamide200–400 mg IV load (200 mg over 15 min), then 100–200 mg q12hSlow Na⁺-channel inactivation — a mechanism you probably have not used yet. NCS 2012 lists it (Class IIb, Level C). Watch the PR interval.
Topiramate200–400 mg via NG, then 300–1600 mg/day divided 2–4× (NCS 2012)Multi-mechanism, including AMPA/kainate antagonism — another glutamatergic lever. No IV form. Causes metabolic acidosis (carbonic anhydrase inhibition) — watch the bicarbonate.
Perampanel4–12 mg/day via NG (loading strategies described up to ~24–32 mg)The only AMPA receptor antagonist — the other up-trafficked receptor. Growing case-series support in SRSE.
Brivaracetam100–400 mg IV load, then 100–200 mg q12hHigh-affinity SV2A. Rapid IV push tolerated.
Phenobarbital (high dose)Titrate to level; NCS notes levels >100 µg/mL have been usedSpecifically useful to prevent withdrawal seizures as a prolonged pentobarbital infusion is weaned — as pentobarbital levels fall, a high phenobarbital level holds the line. NCS 2012 notes the data are limited, so this is a strategy, not a guideline.
Pyridoxine100 mg IV (and gram-for-gram with ingested INH; 5 g empirically if the dose is unknown)Give it. It is cheap, it is harmless, and if this is INH toxicity or pyridoxine-dependency, nothing else will ever work. NCS 2012 recommends IV pyridoxine in young children with epilepsy who develop SE.
MagnesiumBolus 4 g, infusion 2–6 g/h (targets around 3.5 mmol/L reported in SRSE series)Definitive in eclampsia. Outside eclampsia the SRSE evidence is anecdotal — but it plugs the NMDA channel pore, and repleting a low magnesium is mandatory regardless.
3
Immunotherapy — the move that changes outcomes in NORSE/FIRES
Do not wait for the antibody panel to come back
▾

If this is NORSE — new-onset refractory SE with no clear structural, toxic, or metabolic cause — then roughly half of the cases that do get a diagnosis turn out to be autoimmune or paraneoplastic (anti-NMDA receptor, LGI1, CASPR2, GAD65, and the paraneoplastic panel). Antibody results take days to weeks. The window for immunotherapy closes faster than the lab turns around, so treat empirically.

The NORSE/FIRES management consensus recommends starting first-line immunotherapy WITHIN 72 HOURS of onset — before any antibody result is back. If you wait for serology to confirm what you already suspect, you will miss the window. In a disease where almost nothing else has an evidence signal, this is the one intervention with a defensible reason to move fast.
TherapyDoseNotes
Methylprednisolone1 g IV daily × 3–5 days, often followed by an oral taper (~1 mg/kg/day)First-line immunotherapy. Start early in NORSE/FIRES.
IVIG2 g/kg total, divided over 3–5 days (i.e. 0.4 g/kg/day × 5)Given with or after steroids. Watch volume, renal function, thrombosis risk.
Plasma exchangeTypically 5–7 exchanges over 7–14 daysEspecially where an antibody-mediated process is likely. Can be combined with, or substituted for, IVIG.
Rituximab375 mg/m² weekly × 4Second-line, for confirmed or strongly suspected autoimmune encephalitis not responding to first-line.
Cyclophosphamide750 mg/m², monthlySecond-line, often paired with rituximab.
Anakinra / tocilizumabAnakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist); tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antibody)Specifically for FIRES, where a cytokine-driven (IL-1/IL-6) inflammatory mechanism is implicated. The evidence is case series, but it is the most mechanistically-grounded therapy available in a syndrome that otherwise does terribly. Consider early with neuro/rheum input.
Also, in NORSE: look for the tumour. Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis is classically paraneoplastic from an ovarian teratoma — and removing the teratoma is the treatment. Get a CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and a pelvic/testicular ultrasound. This is one of the few places in super-refractory SE where a surgeon can actually cure the disease.
4
The rest of the toolbox — and what does NOT work
Low-quality evidence, honestly labelled
▾
TherapyWhat it involvesEvidence
Ketogenic dietHigh-fat, low-carbohydrate enteral feeding; ketosis usually achieved in 2–3 days. Requires stopping dextrose-containing fluids and steroids where possible.Case series report meaningful response rates in SRSE, including in FIRES. NCS 2012 lists it among alternative therapies. Practical, cheap, low-harm — worth starting early rather than as a last resort, because it takes days to work. Needs a dietitian.
Inhaled anesthetics (isoflurane, desflurane)Delivered via an ICU anesthetic delivery system, titrated to burst-suppression.Effective at suppressing the EEG, but with a high complication rate — profound hypotension, prolonged ileus, atelectasis, and a relapse rate on withdrawal that is close to universal. NCS 2012 notes "high complication rate/morbidity." A bridge, not a solution.
Therapeutic hypothermia32–34 °C for 24 h, added to standard care.NEGATIVE TRIAL. Do not do this for neuroprotection. HYBERNATUS (Legriel, NEJM 2016; n=270) randomized ventilated convulsive-SE patients to hypothermia vs standard care: a good functional outcome (GOS 5) at 90 days occurred in 49% vs 43% (OR 1.22, 95% CI 0.75–1.99; p=0.43). No benefit. Treat fever, but do not induce hypothermia to protect the brain in SE.
Allopregnanolone (SAGE-547 / brexanolone)A neurosteroid GABA-A modulator acting at extrasynaptic receptors — theoretically elegant, because extrasynaptic receptors are not the ones being internalized.FAILED its phase 3 trial (STATUS Trial) in super-refractory SE. A beautiful hypothesis that did not survive contact with a randomized trial. Included here precisely because it is still quoted as promising.
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)Several sessions, typically after other options are exhausted.Case reports only. The paradox (inducing a seizure to stop a seizure) is thought to work by inducing post-ictal inhibition. NCS 2012 lists it — from a handful of cases.
Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS)Acute implantation during SRSE.Case series report seizure cessation in a substantial fraction of acute cases, but the literature is small and heavily publication-biased.
Epilepsy surgeryResection of an identified epileptogenic focus, even acutely.The definitive option when SRSE arises from a resectable focal lesion (e.g. focal cortical dysplasia, a tumour, Rasmussen's encephalitis). Most successful in pediatrics. Worth a serious surgical conversation in any SRSE with a clear structural focus.
CannabidiolPharmaceutical-grade CBD.Established for Dravet/Lennox-Gastaut. Anecdotal use in FIRES. Not standard SRSE therapy.
The two things on this list with a real evidence signal in the right patient are IMMUNOTHERAPY (in NORSE/FIRES) and SURGERY (in a resectable focus). Everything else is case-series-grade. If you find yourself reaching for the sixth item on this table, stop and ask instead whether the diagnosis is right and whether the goals of care still are.
Do not declare futility early. NCS 2012 states plainly that patients have been treated for RSE for weeks to months and gone on to a full functional recovery, and that "the cumulative duration of treatment with continuous infusion AEDs does not appear to be indicative of long term prognosis." The patients most worth persisting with: young, previously healthy, a self-limited cause (e.g. autoimmune encephalitis), and no imaging evidence of devastating injury (e.g. cortical laminar necrosis). Etiology — not duration, not the number of drugs, not the STESS — is what predicts the outcome.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Ready for the floor — ALL of these:
  • Off all continuous anesthetic infusions for ≥24 h, with no electrographic or clinical seizures during and after the wean.
  • cEEG clean for ≥24 h after the infusion stopped — including through the entire weaning trial. (NCS 2012: monitor for 24 h after seizures cease, and during AED weaning trials.)
  • Extubated, or with a secure tracheostomy and a stable ventilator-weaning plan.
  • Off vasopressors ≥12–24 h, MAP ≥65 mmHg without support.
  • Maintenance ASMs at therapeutic levels on an enteral (or reliable IV) route.
  • Mental status improving and a safe airway — able to protect it, adequate cough, swallow assessed.
  • Metabolic house in order: CK falling, K⁺ <5.5, creatinine stable, lactate cleared, no active acidosis.
  • The underlying cause identified and being treated.
NOT yet — keep them in the unit if:
  • Seizures recurred during the wean — that is super-refractory SE by definition, and they need to go back up, not down.
  • Still on any anesthetic infusion, at any rate.
  • Still requiring cEEG for active titration decisions, or on a rate the floor cannot monitor.
  • Still paralyzed — ever.
  • Mental status has plateaued rather than improved, and the reason has not been established (get another EEG, re-image, check an ammonia if on valproate, and reconsider drug accumulation — midazolam's active metabolite accumulates in AKI and produces a wake-up that can take days).
  • Airway is marginal, or there is high aspiration risk with no plan.
  • Vasopressor-dependent, or a new arrhythmia.
  • The cause remains unknown and could be progressive (undiagnosed encephalitis, an evolving mass).
The most common reason a "failed wake-up" is misread as brain death or devastating injury is drug accumulation. Pentobarbital has a context-sensitive half-time measured in days after a long infusion. Midazolam's active metabolite accumulates in renal failure. Before you prognosticate, be certain the drug is out — check levels where you can, allow the time, and get the EEG. Prognostication on a sedated patient is not prognostication; it is guessing, with consequences.

ICU disposition

Floor / step-down

Meets all the criteria above. Continue the maintenance ASM, complete the etiologic workup, start rehab.

LTAC

Prolonged ventilator weaning after a long anesthetic run, tracheostomy, complex medical needs. Expected stay >25 days.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Extubated, medically stable, can tolerate ≥3 h/day of therapy across ≥2 disciplines, with genuine rehab potential.

SNF

Needs 24 h skilled nursing but cannot tolerate 3 h/day of therapy. The common route after prolonged SE in an older patient.

Palliative / hospice

Devastating anoxic injury, progressive underlying disease, or goals that have shifted. Involve palliative care early and in parallel with ongoing treatment — not as the thing you do when you give up.
Pearls

Practice-changing pearls

💡

The fourteen things that actually change what you do

  1. Benzodiazepines are almost always underdosed — this is the #1 error in the disease. Lorazepam is 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg/dose), repeatable once — not "2 mg and see." NCS 2012 attributes mortality of up to 45% to inadequate therapy versus 8% with adequate therapy. Timidity here is not caution; it is a treatment failure with a mortality rate.
  2. Time is the drug's enemy. GABA-A receptors are internalized within minutes while NMDA/AMPA receptors are trafficked in. The benzodiazepine that would have worked at minute 3 fails at minute 40 — not because the dose was wrong, but because the receptor is gone. This one fact explains the entire treatment ladder.
  3. ESETT means you get to choose. Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate are equally effective (47% / 45% / 46%). Therefore pick the one whose side effects your patient can least afford: hypotensive → not fosphenytoin; liver disease or pregnancy → not valproate; generalized epilepsy → valproate. There is no efficacy penalty for choosing safely.
  4. And ESETT's other lesson: half of them will fail. ~53% did not respond to the second-line drug. Have the refractory plan ready before you need it — the airway, the anesthetic, and the EEG. Do not start assembling it at minute 40.
  5. If there's no IV at 5 minutes, the needle goes in the muscle. RAMPART: IM midazolam stopped the seizure before ED arrival in 73.4% vs 63.4% for IV lorazepam — because the IM drug is in at 1.2 minutes and the IV at 4.8. The fastest route wins, not the best drug.
  6. Convulsions stopping ≠ the seizure stopping. Roughly half of patients whose convulsions are controlled have ongoing electrographic seizures; about 14% are in frank NCSE. If they are not waking up within 20–30 minutes, get an EEG. "He's just post-ictal" is the sentence that hides an ongoing brain injury.
  7. A paralyzed patient without an EEG is a total blind spot. Neuromuscular blockade abolishes the convulsion and does nothing to the seizure. If you must paralyze, use a short-acting agent — and the EEG becomes mandatory, not optional.
  8. Check the fingerstick before anything else — and give thiamine before the glucose. Hypoglycemia is a cause of SE that no anticonvulsant will fix. And a glucose load into a thiamine-deficient brain precipitates Wernicke's. The order matters.
  9. A lactate of 10 after a seizure is not sepsis. It is muscle, and it clears within about an hour of seizure control. Do not chase it with bicarbonate, and do not hyperventilate for it. But if it does not clear — that is a genuine signal: ongoing non-convulsive seizure, sepsis, bowel ischemia, or PRIS.
  10. Valproate + POLG/mitochondrial disease = fatal hepatic failure. The single most important "never" in status epilepticus. In an unexplained refractory SE in a young person — especially with any hepatic involvement — do not reach for valproate.
  11. Phenytoin does not treat alcohol-withdrawal seizures. Benzodiazepines do. This is a durable negative finding and a recurring ward error.
  12. Prolactin is a trap. It must be drawn 10–20 min post-event with a baseline, is useless after ~6 h, does not reliably rise in focal or non-convulsive seizures, and a normal value never excludes a seizure. Do not let a normal prolactin talk you out of treating status epilepticus.
  13. A "low" phenytoin level in a hypoalbuminemic patient may be toxic. Phenytoin is 90% albumin-bound and only the free drug is active. Order a free level. The correction equations disagree with each other and are imprecise in exactly the patients who need them.
  14. Do not prognosticate on a sedated patient — and do not declare futility early. Pentobarbital's context-sensitive half-time is measured in days; midazolam's active metabolite accumulates in renal failure. NCS 2012 is explicit that patients treated for weeks can still recover fully, and that the duration of anesthetic treatment does not predict long-term outcome. Etiology does.
The one-sentence version: give a full-dose benzodiazepine fast, move to the second agent without hesitating, assume the seizure is still running until an EEG says otherwise, and hunt the cause like your treatment depends on it — because in refractory status epilepticus, it does.

Refs

Sources & guidelines

Guidelines & consensus statements

  • Neurocritical Care Society (NCS) 2012 — Brophy GM, Bell R, Claassen J, et al. Guidelines for the Evaluation and Management of Status Epilepticus. Neurocrit Care 2012;17:3–23. The source for the definitions, the critical-care timeline, the intermittent dosing table (Table 7), the refractory-SE infusion table (Table 8), the cEEG recommendations, and the prognosis figures used throughout this guide. Full text (PDF)
  • NCS / DGNI 2026 — Guidelines for Neuroprognostication in Critically Ill Adults with Status Epilepticus. Neurocrit Care 2026. The newest guideline on this disease, and it changes the conversation: its systematic review found that "none of the variables and models selected were identified as reliable predictors of mortality in patients with SE" — including STESS, mSTESS, EMSE, age, etiology, SE duration, and even the development of super-refractory SE. It is the source for the prognostication module and for the good-practice statements on counseling surrogates. PMC13053593 · PMID 41507670
  • American Epilepsy Society (AES) 2016 — Glauser T, Shinnar S, Gloss D, et al. Evidence-Based Guideline: Treatment of Convulsive Status Epilepticus in Children and Adults. Epilepsy Curr 2016;16(1):48–61. The source for the time-based treatment algorithm and the Level A benzodiazepine recommendations. PMC4749120
  • ILAE 2015 — Trinka E, Cock H, Hesdorffer D, et al. A definition and classification of status epilepticus — Report of the ILAE Task Force on Classification of Status Epilepticus. Epilepsia 2015;56(10):1515–23. The source for the t1/t2 framework. Epilepsia
  • ACNS 2021 — Hirsch LJ, Fong MWK, Leitinger M, et al. American Clinical Neurophysiology Society's Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology: 2021 Version. J Clin Neurophysiol 2021;38(1):1–29. The source for the ictal–interictal continuum and rhythmic/periodic pattern nomenclature.
  • Salzburg Consensus Criteria for NCSE — Leitinger M, Beniczky S, Rohracher A, et al. Salzburg Consensus Criteria for Non-Convulsive Status Epilepticus — approach to clinical application. Epilepsy Behav 2015;49:158–63; validated in Leitinger M, et al. Lancet Neurol 2016 (sensitivity ~98%, specificity ~90%). Epilepsy & Behavior
  • NORSE / FIRES consensus — Hirsch LJ, Gaspard N, van Baalen A, et al. Proposed consensus definitions for new-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE), febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome (FIRES), and related conditions. Epilepsia 2018;59(4):739–44. Related review (Seizure)
  • USPSTF A & B Recommendations, current as of January 2025 — the source for every grade quoted in the Clinic panel. USPSTF published recommendations
  • FDA prescribing information — KEPPRA (levetiracetam) injection (renal dosing table, max daily dose, IV infusion instructions); VALTOCO (diazepam nasal spray) (the age/weight dose table and repeat rules).

Landmark trials

TrialYearDesign / NResultWhy it matters
VA Cooperative Trial
Treiman et al., NEJM		 1998 RCT, n=384 (overt GCSE), 4 arms: lorazepam vs phenobarbital vs diazepam+phenytoin vs phenytoin alone Lorazepam succeeded in 64.9% of overt GCSE; phenytoin alone was worst (43.6%). No significant differences among the other arms. In subtle SE, no regimen worked well (response rates 7–24%). Established the benzodiazepine — and lorazepam specifically — as first-line. Also delivered the sobering finding that once SE becomes "subtle," almost nothing works — the clearest possible argument for treating early.
PHTSE (prehospital)
Alldredge et al., NEJM		 2001 RCT, n=205, prehospital: IV lorazepam vs IV diazepam vs placebo SE had terminated on ED arrival in 59.1% (lorazepam), 42.6% (diazepam), 21.1% (placebo). Proved that treating SE in the field is better than waiting — and that benzodiazepines do not increase respiratory complications compared with placebo. It demolished the fear that was causing under-treatment.
RAMPART
Silbergleit et al., NEJM		 2012 Double-blind noninferiority RCT, n=893, prehospital: IM midazolam (10 mg; 5 mg if 13–40 kg) vs IV lorazepam (4 mg; 2 mg if 13–40 kg) Seizure stopped before ED arrival, without rescue: IM midazolam 73.4% vs IV lorazepam 63.4% (p<0.001 for both noninferiority and superiority). Median time to active treatment: 1.2 min IM vs 4.8 min IV. Intubation 14.1% vs 14.4%. The route matters more than the drug. Don't burn 4 minutes hunting for a vein — put midazolam in the muscle. Changed prehospital and ED practice worldwide.
ESETT
Kapur et al., NEJM		 2019 Blinded, response-adaptive RCT, n=384 (400 enrollments), benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive SE: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg vs fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg vs valproate 40 mg/kg Seizure cessation + improved consciousness by 60 min: LEV 47%, fosphenytoin 45%, valproate 46%. Stopped for futility — a 1% probability of ever identifying a winner. Fosphenytoin had the most hypotension (3.2%) and intubation (26.4%); valproate the least intubation (16.8%). The most practice-simplifying trial in the field. The three second-line agents are interchangeable in efficacy → choose on comorbidity. And it quantified the bad news: ~53% of established SE fails the second-line drug.
EcLiPSE
Lyttle et al., Lancet		 2019 Open-label RCT, n=286, children, second-line: levetiracetam vs phenytoin No significant difference in time to seizure cessation. Levetiracetam was at least as good and better tolerated. With ConSEPT, it moved pediatric practice toward levetiracetam as a second-line agent — and pre-figured ESETT's conclusion in adults.
ConSEPT
Dalziel et al., Lancet		 2019 Open-label RCT, n=233, children, second-line: levetiracetam vs phenytoin No significant difference in clinical seizure cessation at 5 min after infusion. Independently corroborated EcLiPSE. Two trials, same answer, published together.
HYBERNATUS
Legriel et al., NEJM		 2016 RCT, n=270, ventilated convulsive SE: therapeutic hypothermia (32–34 °C × 24 h) + standard care vs standard care NEGATIVE. Good functional outcome (GOS 5) at 90 days: 49% vs 43% (OR 1.22, 95% CI 0.75–1.99; p=0.43). Do not induce hypothermia to protect the brain in SE. Treat fever, yes — but the neuroprotection hypothesis failed its trial.
STATUS Trial (SAGE-547)
Allopregnanolone / brexanolone		 2019 Phase 3 RCT in super-refractory SE: allopregnanolone (an extrasynaptic GABA-A neurosteroid modulator) vs placebo NEGATIVE — failed its primary endpoint. The open-label series had reported 73% successfully weaned off anesthesia — but in the randomized trial the PLACEBO arm weaned 42.4% of the time. A mechanistically beautiful idea — target the extrasynaptic GABA-A receptors that are not internalized — that did not survive a randomized trial. Its real legacy is the placebo arm: ~40% of super-refractory patients come off anesthesia regardless, so every uncontrolled SRSE case series may be describing natural history. Read the whole SRSE literature through this lens.
DeLorenzo et al.
Epilepsia		 1998 Prospective cEEG cohort, n=164, monitored ≥24 h after clinical control of convulsive SE 48% had persistent electrographic seizures after the convulsions stopped, and 14% were in frank non-convulsive status epilepticus — all comatose, none convulsing. The single most important reason cEEG exists in this disease. "The convulsions stopped" tells you almost nothing. If they are not waking up, they may well still be seizing — and you cannot know without an EEG.
SANAD II (focal)
Marson et al., Lancet		 2021 Open-label noninferiority RCT, n=990, newly diagnosed focal epilepsy: lamotrigine vs levetiracetam vs zonisamide Levetiracetam failed noninferiority vs lamotrigine (HR 1.18, 97.5% CI 0.95–1.47; margin 1.329); zonisamide met it. Lamotrigine had fewer adverse reactions (33% vs 44%/45%) and psychiatric effects (13% vs 30%/23%), and dominated on cost. Lamotrigine remains first-line for focal epilepsy — despite levetiracetam's dominance in hospital practice. The chronic ladder that prevents SE.
SANAD II (generalized)
Marson et al., Lancet		 2021 Open-label noninferiority RCT, n=520, newly diagnosed generalized/unclassified epilepsy: valproate vs levetiracetam Levetiracetam failed noninferiority vs valproate (HR 1.19, 95% CI 0.96–1.47; margin 1.314). "Neither clinically effective nor cost-effective." Valproate remains first-line for generalized epilepsy in men — but its ~10% major malformation rate makes it unusable in those who could become pregnant, which is the central therapeutic dilemma of this syndrome.
Ketamine in RSE
Gaspard et al., Epilepsia (+ subsequent registries)		 2013 → Multicentre retrospective cohort, and subsequent prospective registries, of ketamine in refractory/super-refractory SE Seizure control attributed to ketamine in roughly half of cases, without hemodynamic instability. The observational basis for ketamine in RSE/SRSE — mechanistically the right drug late (NMDA receptors are up-trafficked) and the only one that does not drop the blood pressure. Still awaiting a definitive RCT.

Calculators

  • STESS (Status Epilepticus Severity Score) — MDCalc. Linked out rather than reimplemented: the exact per-option point values are not verifiable from an accessible primary source, and we do not guess at scoring arithmetic.
  • Corrected phenytoin (albumin / renal failure) — MDCalc. Linked out rather than reimplemented: the published coefficients genuinely conflict between sources (0.2 vs 0.25–0.29), and every source agrees a directly measured free phenytoin level is preferable to any correction.
  • The weight-based dose ladder calculator is built in — see the Wards panel. Its arithmetic is fully traceable to AES 2016, NCS 2012 (Tables 7–8), and ESETT.

Scope and limits. This is an educational reference for clinicians in training, not a protocol and not a substitute for clinical judgement or your institution's own guidelines. Every dose and threshold here is traceable to the guideline, trial, or FDA label cited alongside it — but drug availability, formulations, and local practice vary, and the patient in front of you always outranks the table. Where the evidence is weak (most of super-refractory SE), this guide says so rather than papering over it.
